speechtext: The House resumed, from Friday, December 16, consideration of the motion of Mr. Lalonde that Bill C-2, an Act to amend the statute law relating to income tax and to make related amendments to the Canada Pension Plan and the Unemployment Insurance Act, 1971, be read the second time and referred to a Committee of the Whole.

Mr. Speaker, over the years 1 have had the opportunity to participate in debates on amendments to the Income Tax Act. During that period many excellent ideas and suggestions have been made by Members on all sides of the House who have expressed their concern not only about particular clauses in the Income Tax Act, but more often with respect to the administration of the Act. It is a frustrating experience because it is obvious that over the years the various Ministers of Finance, Ministers of National Revenue and their officials have chosen to ignore the comments of various Members. If they had listened they would at least have brought in certain amendments or reorganized their departments in such a manner that we could have a more efficient and more comprehensible tax system.
One of the major problems with income tax in this country is the complexity of the Act. Few people in Canada, including chartered accountants, are able to understand and interpret the Act properly. 1 recall that when the Hon. John Turner was Minister of Finance several years ago-
Who is he?

-he agreed to an amendment proposed by several members who spoke in the House. It was a fairly simple amendment and we anticipated that, when it came in, a short paragraph would cover what had been sought. When it was introduced by the Minister, however, it was two and a half pages long.
It happened that I knew one of the legal officers involved in drafting the amendment and 1 told him that I could not understand why such a simple amendment required two and a half pages when it could easily have been set out in one
paragraph. His response was that we now live in the computer age and that the legislation must be drafted in such a manner that the computer could understand what was being done. A computer has no understanding, Mr. Speaker, but that is what has happened over the years to our tax structure. When a taxpayer is having problems with his assessment or if he has an inquiry, the response to it comes to him in a form printed by the computer. Basically, the taxpayer is communicating with a computer; he is not able to communicate with the individual who is responsible or who should be responsible for taxation.
As has happened in the last year or two, and I assume every Member of Parliament has had the same thing happen, if a taxpayer asks a complicated question or has a serious problem and is able to get some official on the telephone, the response he receives to his query is: "Contact your Member of Parliament". There have been numerous instances where people have phoned me because the tax department has told them to contact their Member of Parliament. But I am not a tax expert. I am not an accountant. It is the responsibility, Mr. Speaker, of those people in the department who are doing assessments to answer some of these questions. However, it seems to me that the officials in the tax department do not now understand the Act. They cannot interpret it. They cannot communicate with the computer. They can only punch in numbers. They have become mechanical. This is the frustration which many taxpayers face when they have problems.
Before I came to this place, when I was practising law, I did considerable tax work. In those days, Mr. Speaker, if a taxpayer had a problem, I could phone the tax department at Regina and tell them the problem. They would tell me to hold for a moment and they would pull the file, and unless the matter was complicated, generally speaking I had the answer within half an hour. If it was complicated, they would say perhaps we should come into the office. You would then make an appointment to go and see them with your client. They would have his income tax returns on the desk and in a matter of an hour the problem would be resolved. That, Mr. Speaker, no longer happens. Those files have been sent to Winnipeg and I believe that has happened in every province in Canada. You cannot get an answer. At least, you cannot get an answer for four, five or six months, if you get an answer then. It is a terrible situation.
I would like to give one example of an elderly gentleman who came into my office two weeks ago. He is on pension. The company which pays him his pension deducts the sum of $100 a month as a tax deduction and, presumably, remits it to the department. The gentleman in question has an RRSP so he

makes instalment payments. He also cashed in an RRSP and the trust company deducted the tax. He was also charged interest on instalments. He did not know what it was for, but he received a bill and he paid it. He later received a receipt showing that he had paid the money, but at the same time, when he paid his instalment, that same amount was taken off his instalment payments.
He was completely frustrated so he telephoned Regina and asked how much he should be paying for instalments because he had been charged interest. He asked: "How much do I have to my credit in my tax account?" He was told, Mr. Speaker: "We do not know; there are four different accounts in your name, apparently". There was one for deductions by his former employer on his pension; one for instalment payments, one for the RRSP and one for instalment interest. They told him they could not bring these accounts together. They could not tell him how much he had to his credit. He asked: "How can 1 calculate my instalments? I do not want to pay interest. You should be able to send me a statement showing what I have to my credit". They told him they could not do it. There are four different accounts, presumably, in the computer and 1 suppose the computer, not being able to think, cannot bring all those accounts together and determine that Joe Blow has x number of dollars to his credit in his income tax account.
I would say, Mr. Speaker, that I hope the Minister of Finance (Mr. Lalonde), the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Bussieres) and the officials of the department will sit down and read the debates in this House and realize what the complaints and problems are as expressed by every Hon. Member of this House. Then perhaps they can make a decision on how to improve our system. Unless that happens, Mr. Speaker, 1 am afraid we are in for some serious trouble in the future.

Mr. Speaker, 1 am pleased in some ways and not in others to participate in the debate on Bill C-2. It is a continuation of the history of both Liberal and Tory approaches towards tax law. It is a corporate welfare budget and it really picks the pockets once again of working Canadians and the poor in this country.
It has been billed as a $4.8 billion recovery program, but when you look at the Bill carefully you see that over the next four years it takes $3.5 billion in increased personal income taxes and an additional $2.4 billion in sales taxes. At the same time, by design, according to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Lalonde) and government Ministers, it will allow plant capacity to remain between 30 per cent and 35 per cent idle and somewhere in excess of 11 per cent unemployment. It is designed to give a little bit of money to the corporate sector to try and keep them quiet, $1.2 billion a year over the next four years, and to ravage $5.9 billion out of the pockets of working Canadians.
1 think Canadians have been amazed for many years, Mr. Speaker, at how unfair and burdensome statute tax law has
become in this country. It was looked at in a 1979 study here in Ottawa which concluded the following:
Furthermore, while there are more than 100 tax breaks open to all Canadian taxpayers, their benefits go overwhelmingly to the wealthy. Almost everyone gets some benefits from such basics as medical and dependent deductions; however, low income Canadians pay a larger percentage of their earnings in taxes than do the wealthy.
The disparity is profound, Mr. Speaker. The study indicated that the exemptions provide roughly 100 times greater benefit for those in the upper income brackets than those at the bottom end of the scale. That means that every time a working person pays $1 in taxes and ultimately gets it back and thinks it is great, some upper income earner gets $100 back. This Government considers that to be fair. The study goes on:
The federal Finance Department acknowledged the situation in a little publicized report called "Analysis of Federal Tax Expenditures for Individuals" which was released in November, 1981. This study concluded that in 1979 the average taxpayer with an income between $10,000 and $15,000 saved $771 on his or her income tax through tax deductions. In that same year citizens with incomes greater than $100,000 managed to save $46,000 in taxes.
That is with the same 100 loopholes. So someone with a $10,000 to $15,000 income saves $771, and those with $100,000 or more get $46,000 back. It goes on:
What is even more striking, said the Finance report, is that there were 740 individuals with incomes over $100,000 who had so arranged their affairs that they paid no federal income tax in 1979.
What kind of a tax system is operating in this country, Mr. Speaker, when that kind of disparity, those kinds of loopholes, are allowed to exist? The answer is easy. It is a system whereby those Members of Parliament sitting on the Government side vote through, or where there is a minority government they manage to con Parliament into voting through, year after year, session after session, Parliament after Parliament, golden gilt-edged loopholes for the wealthy and at the same time simply kick the teeth out of the poor and working Canadians.
Let me give a few more facts which I think home in on the problem. Canadian corporations owe the Canadian Government over $25 billion in deferred taxes. In my own constituency I frequently have Revenue Canada people chase down fishermen, deck hands, out in the bush chasing down some luckers with garnishee orders for this and that, getting them for taxes going back years and years. But how often does the Government encourage their own departments to go out and get back the deferred taxes from corporations? Never, Mr. Speaker. I cannot recall seeing, in the financial pages or in any magazine in this country, any actions taken by either Liberal or Tory administrations to try to get that kind of money back.
It is not only working people who are on wages and salaries who get hurt here, but small business as well. According to Statistics Canada, the average tax rate for large firms is now 24 per cent and for small firms 36 per cent. What kind of fairness is that? You do not have to be a tax lawyer to understand the kind of disparity that has been built into the income tax system in this country. The top 20 per cent of Canadians, as classed by income, now control 70 per cent of
December 19, 1983

the wealth in Canada. One-fifth of Canadians have 70 per cent of the over-all wealth while the lowest 20 per cent in this country now control less than 1 per cent. It is even worse if you set wealth aside. As it stands today, 20 per cent of Canada's highest income group control 40 per cent of the national income every year, Mr. Speaker, while the bottom 20 per cent of the lowest income group have access to only 4 per cent.
In fulfilling its function as a redistributor of wealth, the federal tax system is an absolute failure. With Bill C-2 we once again see the Government, with buildings full of bureaucrats working on Bills such as C-2, failing to address the Canadian economy in any kind of a progressive or fair way.
1 am sure Canadians would be interested to know that the statute law which we are dealing with in today's debate is over 200 pages in length. It changes statute law on income tax, amends the Canada Pension Plan and also amends the Unemployment Insurance Act of 1971. The statute tax law which now exists in Canada literally fills bookshelves. There are literally dozens of feet of this bureaucratic nonsense being spewed out of this House of Commons. In fact, we could introduce into this House and this country tax laws that would fit on to a couple of pages. Anyone in the country could get it and read it and, if it was brought in as progressive kind of income tax, they could say: "At least 1 am being taxed fairly in the same way that the bank manager or the head of Gulf is." In fact, Mr. Speaker, that is not the case at all. This country historically has been, still is, and for some period into the future will be, run in terms of statute tax laws strictly for the wealthy. It takes from the poor, from those on the lower end of the salary and wage scale, 25, 35, 45 per cent and moves it on up the line so that people with $100,000 incomes get $46,000 back when they file their tax in the spring and poor people have to pay.
I would like to give you a few figures, Mr. Speaker, based on the legislation that we are passing. Next year a single taxpayer with a $7,500 income will get a $44 tax break. That is the only break there will be. In 1985 their taxes will jump by $106. The taxes of a single taxpayer with no dependants earning $15,000 will go up next year by $14 and in 1985 by $164. Now we get to the interesting figures; it all starts to come clear again. At the $30,000 income level taxes go up only $36. You have gone up 400 per cent in income but you have not even doubled the amount of increased tax. In 1985 the taxes of the same $30,000 income earner will go up $87. Then we find the real friends that the Liberal Party are after. At an income level of $75,000 this new tax Bill will mean an increase of $250. At $75,000 you are paying almost the same increase as somebody at $15,000. Mr. Speaker, it speaks for itself.
I was interested to listen to the blurred shadow speaking last week. I am glad to see him here today because I know my constituents are always interested in what the blurred shadow from St. John's West has to say on the economy. They are still ruminating on his statement from last year that he and his party would not tell anybody anything about Tory policy because if the Tory Party did that they would never get elected. It has changed a little bit. The Member for St. John's
Income Tax Act
West (Mr. Crosbie) now says that the only way to find out what Tory policies are is to elect the Tories. Then he goes on to say when he is speaking here in the House and when he is being interviewed that if he were in government tomorrow he would continue with the general approach taken by Finance Minister Marc Lalonde.
That comes as no surprise to us in the NDP or to many Canadians from coast to coast. If we look at the voting record of the Liberals and tories on tax law over the last 25 years and how it has been set up, one can see that they have continuously voted together, no matter who is in government, to make sure that the wealthy in this country get the tax breaks so that they will continue to give them lots of money come election time.
I am sorry that I do not have more time. I have all kinds of interesting material to put on the record but I will have to wait until another day.

Mr. Speaker, in contributing to the debate on Bill C-2 today, 1 want to restrict my remarks to the involvement of four principles of accounting and taxation. The first is the accounting principle of matching expenses against revenue. This principle parallels the tax principle that expenses are deductible in so far as they are laid out to produce income.
The second accounting principle is that income is recorded when received or earned. That parallels the tax principle that income is taxed when it is earned or received.
The third accounting principle is that capital cost of an item is to be allocated over the useful life of the asset involved. That parallels the tax principle that capital cost allowances, according to a legislated formula, are to be deducted in computing the income for tax purposes.
The fourth accounting principle is that net income is gross income after deduction of expenses and after providing for all losses. That parallels the tax principle that income for tax purposes is net income after losses.
The first two of those principles which 1 have outlined have been offended by the proposals in Bill C-2. The latter two principles have been offended continually since the 1971 income tax changes which prohibit a loss which is created by capital cost allowance from being deducted from other income. That 1971 erosion was the first blow in destroying the orderly provision of rental housing in Canada.
Today, let us look at the treatment of the other two principles as dealt with in this Bill. The first one affects working mothers and single parents. Under these proposals, these parents are now to be permitted to deduct up to $2,000 in child care expenses per child, to a maximum of $8,000 per family per year. Daycare, which is the most common form of child care expense, today costs about $4,000 per child per year. Even the so-called subsidized daycare centre on Parliament Hill carries a bill of $4,000 per child per year.
I ask the Minister and the House to compare the treatment of working mothers in this respect with the treatment of a

December 19, 1983
Income Tax Act
person who has a business and hires workers to help earn the business income. The wages of workers who are hired to help earn that business income are totally deductible, but working mothers and single parents can only deduct one half of an expense that is every bit as necessary as the wages laid out in the business situation which 1 described.
The Government's proposal of doubling the meagre allowance that has been in effect during the last six years is not the answer. The allowance has been badly eroded by inflation over the past six years. The answer is that child care costs for working mothers and single fathers should be totally deductible as an expense laid out to produce income. In that way, it follows true accounting and true taxation principles.
The other offence created by this Bill is the indexed security investment plan. That proposal offends both principle one and principle two to which I referred. First, interest on money borrowed to invest in Canadian stocks, which is normally deductible, is not now to be deductible even though the dividends which will be received by the taxpayer are to be treated as income in the normal way.
Second, the taxpayer will now be required to include in income in the taxation year one half of the unrealized-I stress unrealized-gain that has accrued during the year. That offends the principle of taxing income as it is earned or received. This might force the sale of securities in order to produce the cash to pay the tax that would be payable, thus upsetting the individual's investment program.
1 concede that something was needed to correct a situation that had existed for some time wherein illusory capital gains attributable to inflation were taxed. 1 think the Government obviously agreed with that or it would not have introduced this Bill at all. This fault had existed not only with marketable securities but also with other assets. 1 suppose one could apply it to any non security type of asset such as a work of art, piece of furniture or a cottage property.
Perhaps the example of a cottage property would most easily illustrate the problem that exists. Imagine two identical properties, one on one side of the lake and one on the other side of the lake. Let us suppose that the owner of the cottage on one side of the lake, which he had owned for a long time, became tired of having the sun set in his face and decided to move across the lake to have the sun rise in his face. He could sell his cottage on his side of the lake but by the time he had realized his capital gain and triggered the tax-there is no rollover provision for that kind of asset-the poor taxpayer would be unable to afford to buy the identical cottage on the other side of the lake. Obviously that is an unfair and unintended treatment but this situation has in no way been addressed by Bill C-2.
The Canadian Institute of Chartered Accountants recently gave a good example of the bad effects of the law on taxpayers who invest in Canadian securities. It produced a table showing that at a zero rate of inflation the effective tax rate on real capital gains was 25 per cent. I believe that was the intent of the original proposals to tax capital gains at all. They were to
include half the gain and then the tax rates would apply so that 25 per cent was the effective tax rate.
Assuming an inflation rate of just 6 per cent, that 25 per cent effective tax rate, coupled with the taxation of illusory capital gains, jumps to 63 per cent. That is hardly a fair tax rate and it is higher than the tax on any kind of income in Canada today. If we go one step further to an assumed inflation rate of 8 per cent, the effective tax rate on a capital gain on Canadian securities owned by a Canadian taxpayer becomes 125 per cent.
What kind of tax system is that? In recent years we have had inflation rates of over 10 per cent, perhaps 11 per cent and 12 per cent. At 8 per cent, the capital gain is taxed away at 125 per cent. Therefore, if a person makes a nominal capital gain of $1,000 of which 8 per cent is inflationary, the real capital gain is $200 but the taxes paid of $250 on the $1,000 nominal gain is a 125 per cent effective tax rate.
Why could the proposals in this Bill not have provided for an adjustment for inflation and for that adjustment to be made at the time of the sale of the securities? That would respect all of the accounting principles for gains when they are realized and for paying tax on income or gains when they are realized. There could have been an adjustment factor built into the calculation based on the period during which the asset was owned, starting from the date of the purchase and ending with the date of the sale. We did not need to have a complex IS IP program to have Canadians do that. The Government has come up with a plan which I can only describe as being a costly, clumsy and complex way of trying to solve a very real problem which could have been solved very much more easily.

It is that time of year again, Mr. Speaker, when the House of Commons is seized with another tax Bill. The speaker from the New Democratic Party helped to remind the House that in December, 1979 there was a budget before this House that had tax provisions in it which accomplished three things. It was a financial plan for the country that was producing new jobs in excess of 30,000 a month and people were coming off the unemployment rolls and into productive participation in the country. It had provisions in it that were reducing rates of inflation and thus reducing the hardship faced by people on fixed incomes who are in difficulty across the nation. It was a financial plan that the national Welfare Council judged to be the fairest financial plan for poor people in Canada that had been produced in the decade of the 1970s. It produced jobs, it reduced inflation and it was fair. It was the fairest budget for poor people in the 1970s.
I was part of that evening in December, 1979 when members of the New Democratic Party joined with members of the Liberal Party of Canada in this House and threw out a government and a budget that would have taken care of the job situation, reduced inflation and was fair to the poor people. It will live in the annals of the history of this country. Canadians will be reminded year after year, month after month, that when faced with a real budget, a real financial
December 19, 1983

plan that did good things for the country and for the poor people, the Liberals and the NDP threw out the government and we have had nothing but chaos, difficulty and trauma ever since.
1 stand in this House today in the full knowledge that Bill C-2 is seen as a minor piece of legislation by the Liberal Government. It contains 210 pages of minor changes to the Income Tax Act. I defy the average Canadian to be able to read it, let alone to comprehend it. I stand here as the representative of Calgary West. I think a lot about taxation.
Yesterday I flew back from Calgary. 1 come from a city that has been devastated and decimated and destroyed by the taxation policies of the Liberal Government following the philosophies of the New Democratic Party of Canada. I come from a city where over 21 per cent of the office space is vacant.
1 come from a city in which over 14 per cent of the rental accommodation is vacant. I come from a city that has an unemployment rate higher than the national average. 1 come from a city that is in that kind of trouble, not because we did not have talented, hard working human beings, willing to take a risk and willing to contribute to the affairs of this nation and to the economy, but because of Liberal tax policies. We have those kinds of people in Calgary with that kind of commitment, but we have a 21 per cent vacancy rate in office buildings, we have bankruptcies and we have devastation of human lives as a direct consequence of one factor and one factor alone, and that is the taxation policies foisted upon us by the Liberal Government with the aid and assistance of the New Democratic Party.
I heard the member from the New Democratic Party talk about corporate welfare bums. In my part of the country in western Canada, and in particular the Province of Alberta, the Liberal Government, for political reasons and political reasons alone, joined with the New Democratic Party to attack one sector of the Canadian economy, namely the oil and gas sector. They went to war with the oil and gas sector using the power of the House of Commons to change taxation policy relating to that sector. This Government went with two hands into the pockets of the people who were producing wealth. This Liberal Government just grabbed and grabbed so much of the production that too little was left in the pockets of those with the skills, the energy and the desire to work. These people were left with so little that they had to shut operations down; they had to quit drilling with their oil rigs. This is a tragedy for the individuals whose lives have been destroyed and it is a tragedy for the country. In the absence of a viable industrial sector, there is nobody to buy the cars, nobody to buy the stoves, nobody to buy the shoes or the products produced in the central part of Canada.
As I look at Bill C-2, with its new taxation policies for the country, changes in some minor areas and in some minor ways, the tragedy is that there is no recognition in this bill for the damage that has been done, in the first instance, to western Canada, but in the broader picture to all of Canada, by previous taxation policies. It would be so much more pleasant to be participating in this debate today if there were provisions
Income Tax Act
in this new legislation to change the situation, to go in the direction of policies which were in place throughout the 1970s.
It would be so much more pleasant to be able to stand in the Chamber and be supportive of the policies that would produce economic health for the region of the country from which 1 come.
Instead, 1 have to stand in this House and bring to the attention of the House that we really do not have in this taxation document anything of significance which attacks the basic problem that exists here today. Our problem is that we have forced far too many people, 1.5 million dedicated, potentially hard working Canadians, into the ranks of the unemployed. That is better than 10 per cent of our labour force. It means that one in ten Canadians is being denied the opportunity to make a contribution to this country through work.
It is a tagedy that we have 210 pages of changes to tax legislation and there is so little in those 210 pages to encourage Canadians to take a risk, to take a chance, to start a business and to contribute. The reason is that we have had a succession of governments that are too easily and too often persuaded that taxation comes first and job creation comes second.
When the members of the NDP stand in this House and talk about corporate welfare bums, do they really understand the significance of what they are saying? They are really saying: Take the money out of the companies first and, if there is anything left over, create a job. How much better would this country be if we said to those individuals and corporations: "Take your money and create jobs". Once that was done, we would have a decent tax base in this country. We would bring in the revenue required to do the kinds of things that need to be done. The NDP and the Liberals should reverse their priorities as quickly as possible.

Mr. Speaker, 1 welcome this opportunity to make a couple of observations. 1 want to go back to the time when, after leaving school, I went to work for the first time. The Income Tax Act was in place, of course. When 1 received my T4 slip, I sat down at the kitchen table, figured out my tax and filed my income tax return. In those days it was very simple. It was not that long ago when as a first-time worker I filed my first income tax return.
In the majority of cases today, people must consult a tax expert because the tax laws are so complicated. 1 know there are Members of this House who, after reading this Bill, would very quickly come to the conclusion that it is full of legalese and is impossible to understand. You cannot understand the implications. In the past six weeks I have received representations from at least two dozen constituents who are having problems with their income tax returns, primarily because they cannot understand all the implications.
Let me give some examples. Two weeks ago a former clergyman came into my office. He had retired approximately two years ago. All of his working life he earned approximately $200 a month and, therefore, never had to file an income tax

Income Tax Act
return. While still in the clergy, his mother left him the family home in Nova Scotia. He converted this home into a place for senior citizens. The cost of running the home is borne by those who live there. There have been between six and ten people living in the home.
In approximately 1973, his lawyer told him that for estate planning purposes he should transfer this home into a holding company wholly owned by himself. Two years ago he was able to secure a teaching position with the Fort McMurray School Board, where he still teaches.
Get the picture. This man is 64 years old, retired from the priesthood, never earned more than $200 per month in all his working life, was left the family home and property by his mother, which he converted to a senior citizens' home. The housekeeper looks after the home for room and board. However, he must pay the taxes and repairs because he does not receive enough money from the seniors at the home. Because he transferred this home to a holding company, the income tax department told him that he is deemed to have made a profit and, therefore, there are taxes owing since 1973. Last July he was hit with a $12,000 tax bill to cover this gain.
Last year he sat down with the income tax collection officer. He did not want to do anything wrong. When he told him he had no money, the collection officer said he would have to pay so much per month. An amount of $350 per month was settled on. This man could ill afford that and at the same time maintain the home in the Maritmes which today provides shelter for six senior citizens.
Two weeks ago the Edmonton tax office, without informing this man, garnisheed $900 per month from his salary. He either has to quit his job and go on welfare, something he would never do, or make an adjustment in his standard of living and sell the home in which these six senior citizens live.
That is not atypical. That is happening all across northeastern Alberta, particularly in the riding of Athabasca. I have received many calls regarding the income tax department moving in like vultures. They appear to have some pre-set plan. They are going to collect the money owing come hell or high water. I attempted to intervene on behalf of this gentleman because of the ignorant and draconian way the income tax department has garnisheed his wages, raising the amount from $350 to $900. When talking to the income tax people in Edmonton I was appalled by their lack of concern, feeling and understanding. They indicated that the taxpayer is constantly lying to them and it is their job to collect this money. Something is wrong when the tax collector moves in on people who are attempting to earn a living, particularly in this case where someone is providing shelter for senior citizens. Obviously this home in the Maritimes is required.
Our present tax system is self-assessing. We have said this time and again. Our whole system is based on that. If Canadians would not sit down at their kitchen tables, fill out their income tax returns and file them with the tax department, our whole system of government would fall apart. However, how are these individuals supposed to understand a tax Bill that is two inches thick and full of legalese, something they cannot
understand? Does anyone think that the lawyer for this gentleman 1 talked about would have transferred this property into a holding company if he thought it was going to trigger an increase in tax? What did it mean to him? It meant nothing. He was a man who did not earn. During the time of his obligation and career, he took a vow of poverty and therefore existed on $200 a month throughout his entire working career. 1 would suggest that early in his career he probably existed on a lot less than that. However, because he had a piece of property that he was able to attain through his family, he transferred it to a holding company. In the ordinary course of events, Mr. Speaker, he would never have done that. We must do something so that the people in the country can assess themselves properly under the Income Tax Act.

Mr. Speaker. I am pleased to speak on Bill C-2, an Act to amend the statute law relating to income tax and to make related amendments to the Canada Pension Plan and the Unemployment Insurance Act, 1971. 1 would like to say that we will have an additional 210 pages added to a booklet that is already over three inches thick and one which many Canadians do not fully understand.
Our Conservative colleagues have spoken about the problems of the oil companies. I would like to relate my remarks to the average Canadian working person and the total unfairness of the amendments which are before us. If I may, I would like to use a few examples. We all know that CP Rail gives $50,000 to the Liberal Party of Canada and to the Conservative Party of Canada and that CP Rail has just received billions of dollars of taxpayers' money through the changes to the Crow rate. However, I would like to speak specifically about some full-page advertisements which are being shown across Canada. We have all seen those advertisements which tell us what a wonderful company Canadian Pacific is. We have all heard the song that says: "I'm a CP Railway man," and we can bet that the Canadian taxpayers are paying for that advertisement.
I would like to tell the House how the discrepancies in the Income Tax Act affect a small farmer in my riding who is losing his farm because of the mortgage rate. That farmer has to leave his farm and go and work somewhere else. However, when he makes money and comes back to try and pay off that mortgage and keep his piece of property, he is told that his farm is not productive and he cannot use it. It is all right for the big companies, through tax loopholes, to be able to sing their songs even though they are not any more productive than the farmer. However, the small farmer needs the extra work so he has gone out, made money and come back and tried to use the money to save his farm, but is told that his farm is not productive, he is not working it and he cannot do that.
If I may, I would like to speak for a moment about taxes paid by waitresses and waiters, a matter which I have already brought up in the House. The income tax department contacted a number of waiters and waitresses in the community of Cranbrook. The assessors went back over three years and

assessed these waiters and waitresses, some of whom are earning just above the minimum wage, up to $2,000 for tips. Those people are being assessed those amounts without any proof that they made those kinds of tips. They do not receive appropriate unemployment insurance benefits because it is not a part of their wage package. If they are laid off, the unemployment insurance that they receive is based upon the very minimum wage that they made. Where is the fairness in our taxation system? We are being asked to make amendments which would change that.
The Minister of Finance (Mr. Lalonde), when he brought down the April 19 Budget, told us that the "comprehensive system of child benefits will be targeted to those who need them the most". The fact of the matter is that the child care expense deduction will only benefit those Canadians who are well above the need level and can afford such expenses. It imposes a cost on the rest of the taxpayers who will pay to rear and educate the children of wealthy parents. People have to be making larger salaries in order to quality for the benefits that exist.
1 have heard the Conservatives talk about how the New Democrats threw them out of government. The fact of the matter is that the Conservative Government was elected on May 5 and did not have the courage to call the House in until October 11, leaving Canadians out in the cold for that whole period of time. It then brought in some policies that the Canadian people would not accept. Conservative members are talking about the poor oil companies in Alberta, but I would like to tell them that there are small businessmen, small farmers, waiters and waitresses out there who are making small wages and, through this Bill, will be carrying the load so that those big write offs can come about.
I think it is unfortunate that we must have a taxation system that is designed to help the wealthy while the lower income earners are the ones who have to foot the bill. We must put a stop to the taxation practices that are taking place in Canada. We must come up with a program which will not only be seen as being fair but will be fair to everyone. We must have a system that will not allow anyone to be able to use the loopholes that this Bill will bring about. This Bill provides for more loopholes so that these large companies will be able to find other ways of not paying their fair share of the running of the Government of Canada. That is wrong, Mr. Speaker. It is wrong that the small wage earners are the ones who have to pay the taxes while the others are able to find and use the big loopholes.
If some people are making as much as $50,000 or $100,000 a year and are not paying one cent in income tax, then surely to goodness we should be looking at that in a very serious way when changing the tax laws. We will not get those kinds of changes from a Conservative government. The fact of the matter is that Conservative governments represent those large lobbyists from CP Rail, the oil companies and the like who come to Ottawa and pick up the phone. I will use the example that was used by the Leader of the Official Opposition (Mr. Mulroney). 1 can see lan picking up the phone and saying: "Is
Income Tax Act
that you, Brian? We have a problem here. We need a few more loopholes".
Or I can see him picking up the phone and calling the present Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau). We all know that that will take place whether we have a Conservative government or a Liberal government. That will not help the average Canadian.
Let me ask you, Mr. Speaker, where are the lobbyists for waiters and farmers? Those lobbyists cannot afford to come here and lobby the Government to bring about the kinds of changes that they want. If we are going to have these kinds of changes, they will be made by the New Democratic Party. They will be made by a Party that represents the people of Canada and not the oil companies or CP Rail or the big multinational corporations. Until we get those kinds of changes and bring about those kinds of amendments, we will not have fair taxation practices in Canada. The average worker in Canada will continue footing the bill, whether it be under the banner of the Conservatives, the British Columbia Social Credit Party or the Liberals in Ottawa. That is the kind of legislation that is coming forward now, and we in this Party will fight it all the way.
We in this Party believe that there must be fairness, and the only way there will be fairness is by recognizing that everyone has to pay his fair share. There should be fairness in the legislation and the Government of Canada should decide how the money will be spent without allowing CP Rail to put a full-page advertisement in the newspapers telling us how proud it is of its history.

Mr. Speaker, I listened with a great deal of interest to the member from the NDP who suggested solutions that will not work. The most important change that should take place but which has not been addressed in Bill C-2, an Act to amend the Income Tax Act, is one that should create more productivity in the economy and more wealth in the country. The present tax system has been bleeding the economy at every level. We can argue back and forth about divisions in the country, and some were referred to again today, but the real problem is that the present Income Tax Act is counter-productive.
I want to give a few examples of this, Mr. Speaker. In the wheat growing districts of the country today, the tax burden is so unbearable that farmers do not deliver grain but keep it in their bins. That is serious. They do not get the same tax breaks that other areas of the economy enjoy. I believe figures were given regarding the larger corporations, but small farmers and small businesses are facing a taxation burden that is counterproductive. Until this problem is solved we cannot solve some of the other very serious economic problems in the country.
Ten or 15 years ago it was quite easy for any farmer, businessman or working person to fill out an income tax return, but today it is absolutely necessary to hire an accountant at a cost of $250 or $400 to interpret the Act and fill out the form. As well, the interpretation depends a good deal on

December 19, 1983
Income Tax Act
the adjuster who looks the form over. Clarification is needed in this area which at present is most unfair.
We had good examples of interpretation and of long-term planning in the Budget brought down by the former Minister of Finance which was an absolute calamity for agriculture and small business. It is necessary for farmers to be able to set up a long-term retirement savings plan, if you will, while still operating the family farm. The Minister of Finance (Mr. Lalonde) introduced drastic changes that would make this very difficult for many farmers, particularly those engaged in raising livestock. The Department of National Revenue should look into this problem.
The capital gains tax is another critical area of concern. I spoke on this subject once before in the House and an Hon. Member opposite attacked me with vigour. Mr. Speaker, the Liberal Party has promised to address the valuation date in 1971 in the last three elections but there has been absolutely no change in the legislation, which is outdated and not in step with reality. This should be corrected but there is no mention of it in the Bill.
Long-term planning is very important. If we are to have a productive society, farmers and small business people must be able to make long-term plans that they can depend upon. Lack of this creates confusion in the economy and is counter-productive. We are finding that the rules are changed mid-stream. In Estevan, for instance, a concrete company was operating under a particular set of rules but then the percentages were changed and it found it came under a mining provision which made its operation more expensive. Many small businesses have run into difficulties because the Act was not clear. It should be a top priority of the Department of National Revenue to make the conditions of operation more clear and make it possible for farmers and small businessmen to plan their operations.
There is a non-productive aspect to the Income Tax Act as well. In my own operation I have had employees on the payroll for years but I find that the terms of the Income Tax Act do not offer any incentive for an employee to work overtime. When someone gives $2 to the Government and only keeps $1 for himself and incurs the usual expenses of going to work, there just is no incentive to work longer hours.
Inflation has created major problems for small businessmen and farmers. They simply cannot keep up with it and the Income Tax has not been adjusted to meet this problem.
Another area of concern is arrangements for retirement savings plans. The rules have been changed for people engaged in agriculture and now they just do not understand them. Indeed, I have on file two or three letters from accountants who do not even understand the rules, so how can the layman be expected to?
Earlier today the Hon. Member for Moose Jaw (Mr. Neil) spoke of the computer age. We have, with the Income Tax Act, found ourselves circulating paper. It almost takes a team of accountants to fill out one's income tax return. The computer age has complicated the system and by all indications it is going to be complicated even further.

The importance of addressing this serious problem immediately must be realized by the Government. If these areas are not addressed, we will see a continued decline in productivity and no incentive on the part of the people to go out and produce so we can afford those things in life which we would like to have. We must continue to produce so the Government can afford to address those areas of responsibility which certainly should be high in priority. Unless we address the Revenue Department and the Income Tax Act in a major way, Mr. Speaker, in order to bring under control some of the serious inequities which are there, this country faces problems.

Mr. Speaker, I am happy to have the pleasure of taking part in this debate because it gives me a chance to restate some of the points I was trying to make in question period on Wednesday of last week; that is, that the collections branch of the Department of National Revenue does not know what the appeals branch is doing, and vice versa. In other words, the left hand does not know what the right hand is doing. One assesses and the other collects, and like so much of what the Liberal Government gets involved in, there is no modicum of realization of where they are going.
The most important element in this debate is not income tax per se, or the payment of such. We all realize that it is here to stay. It is not that income tax is a so-called temporary measure, temporary to the extent that it was initiated during the First World War and is "temporarily" still with us, with the crushing effect it is having on Canadian business and the Canadian taxpayer.
There are some 120 changes in this Bill, Mr. Speaker, and, of course, the Bill emanates from the April Budget. It is now coming to fruition only in December, another eight months record which we are so used to seeing in this House. The best part of the Bill, in my view, is the investment tax credits, because the cash flow and capital accounts of small businesses have been decimated by the recession. I am appalled, as is the Hon. Member for Waterloo (Mr. McLean), at the removal of the $100 charitable donation deduction, which is nothing more than an unmitigated tax grab by the Government of $80 million to $100 million.
However, the greatest issue, which has been pointed out by most of my colleagues, is the complexity of the income tax system. The next most grave issue, in my view, is the attitude of the collectors of the tax themselves and the heavy-handed collection tactics which have been used in the past few years. This is something we have never had happen before. We now have a tremendously high rise in reassessments. It is noteworthy in this regard to tell the House that my accountant has had to deal with more reassessments this year than in many of the last years combined. This is due, I suppose, to the fact that the tax department seems to have upped its quotas. I say "quotas" advisedly, but we on this side of the House under-
December 19, 1983

stand that that is exactly what has happened. How much tax justice can Canadians really expect from a department which is running a quota system?
The Government professes to believe in the value of the small business sector. Then it turns around and administers the Income Tax Act to the detriment of that very vital sector. When it comes time to harass and reassess-and both terms are becoming increasingly interchangeable and synonymous with the department-the owner of a small business is deemed to be guilty until he proves himself innocent. That is a radical departure from Canadian justice, in my view. It is a situation in which we cannot be proud, especially in light of the new Charter of Rights and Freedoms. Of course, that does not seem to apply to the operations of the tax department, as the Minister invoked the "notwithstanding" clause for his Department. Tax justice is really what we are after and this Bill does not give us very much help.
We are driving Canadians to the brink of financial disaster and in the process are denying them their fundamental rights. When a small businessman wants to appeal his assessment, he must first appeal, then he must make payment, thereby implying some kind of guilt. The process then begins. Is it any wonder that Canadians are disgruntled? It is a long and often costly process and throughout it all a small businessman's cash flow is tied up. Many of them will not appeal a small assessment because they cannot afford the court costs. 1 do not consider this justice.
This is how the contribution of small businesses to the Canadian economy is recognized. 1 would like to hear from the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Bussieres) when he has the time-I realize he is very busy in his new-found role of Jesse James without a gun-as to why he is out to harass Canadians with reassessment quotas and inefficient administration of his Department.
However, to get back to the basic problem, the system is too complex, purely and simply, and that is why we are running into increasingly difficult situations in the administration of the Act. The amendments being brought forward by this legislation are a start, to be sure. We all recognize that. However, do they go far enough and do they really address the fundamental principles? I think not.
The Chamber of Commerce warns that the complexity of the Income Tax Act could loose an underground economy. In its brief to the federal Government a number of recommendations were made covering a wide range of areas which should be reformed. These are worthy of consideration. However, before any fundamental changes are made, perhaps we should have a moratorium on amendments to the Income Tax Act until we know exactly where we want to go. That was mentioned by this side of the House in the Crow debate, but to no avail.
This tinkering with different parts of the Act here and there is not really going to address the very real problems which Canadians are experiencing, the problems 1 have been hearing about every day in my constituency office. For example, a man who borrows $30,000 to invest in a business writes off the
Income Tax Act
interest on that loan and then is assessed. He has to appeal. He sends in eight post-dated cheques. In the meantime his cash flow is nil and he will probably face bankruptcy. The Act was to implement a temporary source of revenue to help the Government through the war years, but obviously it is much more than that now. Changes must be made to reflect what the income tax has become and the purposes for which it is being used. We need a major re-examination of the Income Tax Act, and until that is done we should stop tinkering with it. We seem to be doing more harm than good in most cases. In the meantime Canadians continue to suffer injustices.
Mr. Lyman Maclnnis, who is the senior partner in Touche Ross and Company and President of the Institute of Chartered Accountants of Ontario, 1 believe has said it much better than any of us could. In a speech he made recently he talked about the incomprehensibility of the Act. He said, and 1 quote:
Now, I'm not going to pick out sections of the Act that deal with rare corporate re-organizations or the like. No! I'm going to deal with ordinary, every-day applications-things that affect ordinary, individual taxpayers.
Let's start with Section 56(1 )(s). As a matter of fact, if 1 want to be completely correct, in the Income Tax Act that's not a section at all. It's a paragraph. If it was just plain old 56-that would be a section. If it was 56(1), that would be a sub-section. But, because it's 56(1 )(s), that makes it a "paragraph" under the scheme of the Income Tax Act. And you have to know that in order to find your way through this mess.
Oh yes, and before 1 can even quote you what paragraph 56(1 )(s) says, you have to remember that Section 56, itself, begins with the words:
"Without restricting the generality of Section 3, there shall be included in computing the income of a taxpayer for a taxation year-" and you find that about five pages earlier than where paragraph 56(1 )(s) begins. So, the whole quotation is:
"Without restricting the generality of Section 3, there shall be included in computing the income of a taxpayer for a taxation year, the amount of any grant received in the year under a prescribed program of the Government of Canada relating to home insulation or energy conversion by the taxpayer, other than a married taxpayer who resided with his spouse at the time the grant was received and whose income for the year is less than his spouse s income for the year, or the spouse of the taxpayer with whom he resided at the time the grant was received, if the spouse's income for the year is less than the taxpayer's income for the year to the extent that the amount is not required by paragraph 12(1 )(u) to be included in computing his or his spouse's income for the year or a subsequent year".
Do you know what that really says, Mr. Speaker? It says, according to Mr. Maclnnis:
-if you receive a home insulation or energy conversion grant you have to include it in income, unless your spouse has higher income, then he or she has to report it.
Mr. Maclnnis says that is convoluted garbage and 1 agree with him. He goes on with many more examples, Mr. Speaker, section by section, of this convoluted garbage. I think you can see exactly what the Canadian taxpayer is faced with. The entire Income Tax Act was revamped in 1972, not really that long ago. The so-called reform of the Act was supposed to give us a well thought out and simpler tax system. However, since 1972 there have been more than 30 major amending Acts. There were 350 changes in 1980-81 alone, and now we have 120 more here. Two months ago the Minister of Finance (Mr. Lalonde) introduced 133 more amendments.

December 19, 1983
Income Tax Act
Mr. Macinnis is one of the top people in this field and the essence of his argument is simply this:
The wasted manpower and dollars spent in trying to understand it and comply with it-forget the waste in trying to get around it-the wasted productive time and money spent in simply trying to comply with it, is enormous.
He makes two points which I agree with and which I think other people in this House do. He says:
1)	put a hold on tax changes for a period of eighteen months to two years, so
that we can get caught up with what has been happening to us over the last
few years;
2)	re-write the existing Act so that it is understandable by human beings with
average intelligence.
That is you and 1, Mr. Speaker, I would presume.

speakeroldname: Hon. Flora MacDonald (Kingston and the Islands):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as has been said by a number of people who have taken part in this debate, if there is one thing which unites Canadians it is the fact that they all agree the Income Tax Act is the most complex and difficult piece of legislation to understand which exists in the country. Whether you happen to be from the east or the west, the north or the south, whether you are French speaking or English speaking, whether you are a Canadian whose family has been here for generations or you are a new Canadian, all agree it is terribly difficult to understand or come to grips with the complexities of the Income Tax Act. Even those who are supposed to be experts in this field, whether it is tax lawyers or accountants, actuaries or financial analysts, all agree you simply cannot find your way through the maze of complexities of the Income Tax Act.
I say it is difficult to understand, but if there is one thing that Canadians do understand, Sir, it is that the Government is trying to make a tax grab at their expense. This is being done in the amendments to the Income Tax Act which we have before us at this time. It is being done in the area dealing with charitable organizations, the voluntary sector in our society. It is being done. Sir, in a disguised way. The Government is putting forward these proposals as something which will benefit Canadians. But when you look at it then you see that it is anything but.
These proposals put forward by the Government have been condemned outright by the National Voluntary Organizations. When they were first put forward, not in this Budget but in the last one, they said:
The Coalition has proposed that the Minister of Finance eliminate the standard $100 deduction and replace it with a 50% charitable tax credit as an option to the current deductibility provisions for charitable giving. This reform would create an incentive for all taxpayers to support their voluntary groups and would make the incentive equitable between income groups. (The Government) failed to implement this proposal, known as Give & Take-
The chairman of the National Voluntary Organizations, lan Morrison, said at that time:
There is no equity for Canadian charities in ... the budget.
He went on to say that the Minister:
-said his goal was to improve fairness and equity in the tax system, but the changes he has proposed in tax treatment of charitable giving will increase
inequity by benefiting only the most affluent taxpayers, those in the top one per cent of tax brackets.
What the Government has done is to take half the recommendations made by the National Voluntary Organizations and other groups and agreed to eliminate the standard $100 deduction available to all taxpayers, but did not agree to implement the 50 per cent charitable tax credit also proposed. This is going to have a very negative impact on charitable organizations throughout the country.
1 remind you, Sir, that the voluntary sector of our society is big business in Canada. It involves some three million Canadians. Just to give you an idea of some of the facts which underline what I mean by it being a big business, there are
47.000	charitable agencies in this country. They involve the voluntary work of three million Canadians. They employ some
200.000	Canadians on actual payroll staff. These charities took in $5.6 billion in 1980, equivalent to 11 per cent of all federal Government revenue or almost 2 per cent of GNP. Their wage and benefit bill was almost $2 billion in 1980. That represents 1.6 per cent of employed workers in Canada, twice as many as are directly employed in forestry or one quarter of all employed in public administration by all levels of government. Almost three million Canadians volunteered almost 400 million hours of work in 1980. This is very big business indeed, yet the Government is moving to penalize and stifle the voluntary sector by the proposals it has put before us.
1 am sure every Member of Parliament has had letter after letter from voluntary organizations and individuals across this country, indeed from their own constituency, appealing to their humanity and sense of fairness, their sense of justice, not to implement only one-half of the proposals put forward by the Naitonal Voluntary Organizations. That is what the Government is doing with these budget day proposals. Instead of implementing the "give and take" proposals, they are implementing only the take end and not looking at the giving end. That is what so many Canadians are now protesting.
I have a letter from a gentleman in my own riding writing on behalf of the Incorporated Synod of the Diocese of Ontario to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Lalonde), and he says:
On a positive note, there is undoubtedly general approval of your decision to eliminate the $100.00 deduction. It is felt that, if anyone cares enough about their charitable giving, the amount will be considerably in excess of $100.00. Such people are in no way penalized by the elimination of the standard deduction.
Having said that, however, it must be admitted that there is widespread disappointment at your failure to do anything about the proposal for a tax credit. To have implemented this would have been a practical gesture of encouragement to those who take their charitable giving seriously.
The work of the churches is, for all practical purposes, entirely dependent upon voluntary donations. Increasingly, our budgets are obliged to include items which may be classed as social service .. . With these thoughts in mind it is our hope that you will reconsider the matter of a tax credit.
Of course, it is not there in the Budget. Another lady writing me, again from Kingston, says:
I am a retired R.N., single, and a woman. Therefore, I am not wealthy.
December 19, 1983

That goes without saying in those circumstances, Mr. Speaker. She continues:
I like giving to certain charities. 1 find that with the present rules regarding charity giving, wealthy people can give more to charity and also get a better reduction on their income tax. If the rules were changed so that charity donations were deducted from tax instead of from taxable income this would even things out.
One of the adverse measures of this Bill, Mr. Speaker, is that it really does nothing to stimulate the voluntary sector. It stifles the voluntary sector. It does not expand its operations; it reduces its operations.
1 will close by saying that instead of encouraging Canadians to want to contribute to the well-being of their neighbours and to the country as a whole, and particularly at this time of year when Canadians want to make donations, this Bill is saying to them that if they do it in the way that the Government is proposing they will be penalized, not encouraged.

Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to rise, particularly after the Hon. Member for Kingston and the Islands (Miss MacDonald) spoke. I find 1 often agree with many points which she raises. It is too bad she is not the Leader of the Progressive Conservative Party. Perhaps we would have some more humane policies in the future.
Her reference to the complexities of the Income Tax Act particularly remind me of some of the people in my riding who have great concern every time income tax time rolls around. I refer particularly to the many thousands of new immigrants in my riding who do not speak English as their first language, who do not understand the income tax forms and certainly must be extremely confused about the income tax policies. As a result they often have to rely on very expensive advice which they really cannot afford. 1 appeal to the Government to make sure that there are some programs in place to help these kinds of people, and also low income people, have access to free income tax advice. In the past we have seen how some community organizations have provided this service, often training their own people. It is a good job-creation program.
I would also like to mention a concern that has been brought up repeatedly by the National Anti-Poverty Organization. That is the concern about usurers who are only too ready to bilk the poor. In particular, there are a number of loan companies that, I understand, will advance child tax credit returns early in the year when families are desperate to have this money for survival. They, of course, charge very high rates of interest for this service. That is another area that we would like the Government to give some attention to.
I would like to speak to Bill C-2, Mr. Speaker, from primarily a social policy perspective. The last Liberal Budget catered to corporate Canada at the expense of the average income earners. It ignored the needs of poor people and increasing numbers of unemployed people completely. The theory was a nice, comfortable Liberal theory that this would increase productivity and create more jobs. We know now that this has not happened to any great extent. Unemployment remains high and businesses are the winners as far as the tax system is concerned.
Income Tax Act
Bill C-2 will do little to reverse this trend. It will add a burden to Canadians when it should be providing relief for the Canadians that are hardest hit by the economic situation of Canada as well as by the unfair tax policies of this Government. The tax changes which we would have favoured would have stimulated our economy, put more money in the hands of consumers and provided tax incentives for people to purchase needed goods which they have avoided purchasing during the last period of recession. This would help small businesses considerably.
It is deplorable, Mr. Speaker, that this Government continues to support a tax policy which overtaxes middle income people, their own supporters to some degree, provides very few tax credits for low income people, and allows many millionaires to pay no income tax at all. It just seems inconceivable and hypocritical that the Liberal Party and the Liberal Government refuses to change any of the multiple tax loopholes which allow this situation to exist. If the Liberals are bad, just think what it is going to be like if the Tories get into government.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: Awful. You are right.
The only solution, of course, is to elect an NDP government.
Hear, hear!

Most Canadians would agree that we need a fair tax system and that this should be the Canadian Government's goal. I am sure most Canadians would feel this, Mr. Speaker. Why do the Tories and the Liberals not respond to this? Why do they not accept this as a goal and try to make some major reforms? This Bill does not do anything in the way of reform. It may do a few token things here and there, but it does nothing to relieve the basic problems of a tax system which is undemocratic and unfair. Incomes under our present system are not evenly distributed in Canada. There has been no change in this direction. The Government has not got the guts to make any major reforms.
Both the Liberals and the Tories ignore the increasing poverty in our society. They refuse to redistribute wealth through a progressive tax system or to guarantee minimum incomes. Income distribution has remained static in Canada over the last 10 years. There has been no change in the figures. Twenty per cent of the highest income earners control 40 per cent of the national income, the wealth of this country. If we compare that with the lowest income group, 20 per cent of the population in our lowest income group, have access to only 4 per cent of the national income. Is that in any way just or fair, Mr. Speaker?
There is no fairness.

We can go back back to that old cliche, which is certainly the theme of this Government that "the rich get richer and the poor get poorer". The poor are increasing in numbers every day in this country.

December 19, 1983
Income Tax Act
A just federal tax system should compensate those who are least able to cope with the current economic problems, Mr. Speaker. It should not only provide deductions for the cost of food and fuel in the north-subsidies would be an even better system-but it should also have a tax credit system so that native people who live in the north and do not depend on a cash economy so much would have the benefits and some protections.
In this Party we have long advocated a cost of living tax credit for low income people. This would be a very good time to try to implement that policy because inflation is lower. It would not cost that much to do it and it would build in a protection for people with a flexible indexing tax credit system which would really help poor people and those on fixed incomes, many of them senior citizens.
Bill C-2 is unjust, Mr. Speaker. It does not deal at all with the basic injustices in our tax system. I would like to give you a couple of other examples. Nearly 300 people who earn over a quarter of a million dollars a year pay no income tax. Is this just? Is it just that over 8,000 people who make in excess of $50,000 a year pay no income tax to the Government? Is it fair or just or even financially feasible that many profitable corporations such as the Bank of Montreal make millions of dollars in profits even in times of depression or recession and pay no income tax? It seems to me that this wealthy elite in our Canadian society must bear the major responsibility for the enormous deficit that we have in Canada today.
A progressive and just tax policy should reflect social goals, not only financial considerations. We believe that a fair tax system should redistribute wealth in an equitable way. We on this side also believe that a progressive tax system is essential to provide a form of social investment that will not only benefit individuals who need help and are hardest hit in our society but will also ensure that we have enough money to finance essential social programs.
For example, we in Canada tend to plan most of our programs from an economic point of view. We do not look at the investment in human resources and social programs. We need reforms to tax provisions for families. We can look at the regressive deductions for child care, spousal deductions and deductions for children and can see the progressive kind of policies which we have for family allowance and child tax credits. We need to review this situation and put it into a more progressive and general framework.
There are many other social policies I could deal with but I regret that 1 do not have enough time. We agree completely with the criticism of the removal of the $100 deduction for charitable donations and the complete neglect of the give and take proposals of the National Voluntary Organizations. We would like to see a reform of charitable organizations and how they are defined as well.
I see that my time is up. I had many proposals which this Party would put forward. I hope the Government will consider them in developing a more just tax system and major reforms
to redistribute wealth in this country and accommodate social needs.

Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to rise to participate in this tax debate. Before I begin my remarks, 1 think I should thank the former Minister of Finance, who is now Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. MacEachen), and the present Minister of Finance (Mr. Lalonde) for accomplishing something during their four years of responsibility of being Finance Minister, which is having Canadians become more involved in the political process than ever before. They have suddenly paid attention to what is going on in this Parliament with our taxation policy. Canadians have tended to sit back and have great faith in their governments and the tax system without becoming too involved in the process of taxation policy. I can say without any doubt that November, 1981 will go down in the annals of the history of this country as the time when people became involved in the development of their taxation system. I have never had such reaction to any tax proposals or any proposals whatsoever in all my life. Not only did people become involved, they became very aware of what a rotten job the Government is doing with taxation policy. I suggest the Government's taxation policies also helped the deficit of the post office somewhat as a result of the letters being sent to us from throughout the country as well as the lobbies that began to take place. Therefore I want to thank those Ministers for getting the Canadian people involved in what is happening in the taxation process. It is obvious that the people in my riding of Brampton-Georgetown as well as the constituents of my colleagues are not happy with what is happening.
The Bill before us is one that the Progressive Conservative Party will vote against. While there is no question that there are good measures in the Bill, there are also a lot a tax increases which Canadians will not even realize until they begin filling out their tax forms. They will not realize these tax increases in the spring of 1984 but right after the election in 1985 when they begin filling out their tax forms at that time. Canadians will not realize until 1985 that the Minister of Finance has raised their taxes. That is the sneaky part of this Bill which reflects this part of the Budget-the recovery Budget, he calls it-that he brought in in April. The Minister's nickname for the Budget is the recovery Budget, and while there will seem to be a recovery in 1984, Canadians will start paying increased taxes in 1985. If we are going to see any recovery in 1984 it will be defeated by what will happen in 1985 when Canadians begin paying those additional taxes.
The Government has been operating with smoke and mirrors for the last four years. After four years of this Government the people of this country are saying that they made a big mistake in 1980. The Hon. Member for Mississauga North (Mr. Fisher) is shaking his head in utter disgust at what 1 am saying, but I saw the poll results from his riding. I would be shaking my head too right now. As a matter of fact, I would be extremely worried about my policita! career. The average life of an MP is five years and nine months. He is not even going
December 19, 1983

to make it. Being associated with the Minister of Finance will not help him at all. It will hinder him.
The deficit is an issue that has not been properly addressed. People do not understand the deficit because when they hear about the amount of money involved no one, even CP, can relate to it. The deficit is in the billions of dollars. We are currently in debt for some $130 billion and if we were to make a determined effort to pay back that money which the Government has borrowed at $1 billion a year, without any interest it would take 130 years to pay it back.
The Government has indicated that it cannot really worry about the deficit right now because we are going through tough times. One of the most staggering statistics in this country is that 75 per cent of all the borrowing done in Canada is by governments. This allows the private sector to borrow only 25 per cent of the available capital. The municipal, provincial and federal governments are borrowing 75 per cent of all the available loan money, which means that interest rates will remain high. Governments can afford to pay a little more because they simply tack it on to the deficit which another government may pay later on. However, the private sector is left to scramble for the remaining 25 per cent. This situation does not lead to a recovery.
1 believe it is very important for a government to approach the method of reducing that deficit in a business-like manner. There are many examples of how this can be done. There was a recent report on the restaurant operation in this place which indicates that we can save $2 million in a year. It is the most scathing report to be released around here in a very long time. As well, that is a very small part of the operation of government.
I see by the Sergeant-at-Arms walking toward the Table that my time is up. Let me say in conclusion that this Bill contains many flaws. When it comes time to vote and proceed into Committee of a Whole this afternoon, the Progressive Conservative Party will vote against it. I want to say to Canadians that relief is on the way because this is the last tax Bill that they will have to put up with before the Progressive Conservative Party forms the next government and presents a realistic budget for the Canadian people.

speechtext: Madam Speaker, in the National Assembly, the PQ majority is about to, if it has not already done so, adopt Bill 38 aimed at withdrawing from municipalities the funds they may have received directly or indirectly from the Government of Canada. After postponing the session of the National Assembly for a month, supposedly to prepare Quebec's economic recovery, the PQ Government found nothing better to do than to prevent municipalities from receiving funds that could be used to improve the well-being of the people of Quebec and put the Province on the road to recovery. The Government of Canada is being accused of distributing funds arbitrarily. In fact, Bill 38 is a prime example of arbitrary and discretionary action, since the Minister of Municipal Affairs may even decide whether or not the legislation is to be enforced. This kind of legislation is one of the reasons why the new Parti nationaliste and its leader, Mr. Marcel Leger, are not meeting with a great deal of enthusiasm.
