Madam Speaker, people of Canada, now hear this! The policies of the Liberal Government are setting the stage for unwarranted increases in the cost of food. I ask the Government how our farmers are going to stay in business with higher transportation costs brought about by its Bill C-155, higher fuel and higher fertilizer costs brought about by the National Energy Program, to say nothing about the doubling of machinery costs?
While the expenses of the farms go up and up, the returns to the farmers go down and down. In 1977 barley sold for $2.80 per bushel; in 1983 it is $2.50 per bushel. A 500-pound steer sold for 85 cents a pound in 1977, and it is still only 85 cents per pound. In the meantime the price of beef, bread and milk, almost every essential item of food, to the consumer, has increased three to four times.
The farmer is getting less and this Government is grabbing much of the increase. No wonder more and more of our farmers go bankrupt every year. If this trend continues, with the cost of everything the farmer buys increasing and almost

December 19, 1983
everything the farmer sells decreasing, farmers will not be able to stay in business and we will soon have socialized farms, and then the people will really pay right through the nose for their food. Is this the aim of this Government? Heaven help us if it is!

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Transport
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I rise today on behalf of my constituents to draw special attention to the efforts of the Government to protect and nurture the multiculturalism element of our country. No country in the world has been more tolerant of physical and cultural differences than Canada. No country has been more receptive to the plight of immigrants in modern times. Through the Speech from the Throne, the Liberal Government demonstrated that the pursuit of these qualities will continue to be a priority.
The Minister of State for Multiculturalism (Mr. Collenette) last week announced that he will introduce new legislation to give legal recognition to the Government's multiculturalism policy. As well, Madam Speaker, most of the requirements for Canadian citizenship will be relaxed for immigrants over 65 years of age. The Liberal Government will also continue to encourage a wider use and knowledge of the country's two official languages and will provide support to' the voluntary sector in over a thousand language instruction projects that will help 125,000 people.
We will also give early attention to the report of the parliamentary Standing Committee on Visible Minorities, and we will strengthen the law against hate literature. It is the commitment of this Government to fight for equality for all people living in Canada. The contributions of this country's multicultural groups have enriched our society, making Canada a better country in which to live. Variety, civility and tolerance are characteristics of this country that will be treasured and nurtured by the Liberal Government.

Madam Speaker, at Tuesday's "Last Liberal Command Performance" the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) told the dinner gathering that a nation's strength is not due to the size of its armies or its balance sheets, but to the size of its heart. It has become painfully obvious that the Prime Minister subscribes whole heartedly to that view. His heart is not in either defence or economic issues.
When his Government took office in 1968, the net debt was $17.7 billion. When we started this fiscal year, it stood at $120
billion. He has cut the heart out of our nation's financial stability.
In 1968 the proportion of our Gross National Product devoted to defence stood at 2.4 per cent. By 1973 it had plummeted to 1.6 per cent, and now it stands at about 2 per cent, the second lowest in NATO, the alliance from which the Prime Minister attempted to withdraw. That is heartbreaking. But what was most disheartening of all last Tuesday was to hear the Prime Minister refer to those "pipsqueaks in the Pentagon", when it is apparent that he is more comfortable with his comrades in the Kremlin.
Is this how political will is injected into arms negotiations? Is this how a Canadian leader tries to win the support of our greatest friend and ally? No. What we have here is third rate, third level diplomacy. Have a heart, Mr. Prime Minister. Call an election, and let Canadians give their hearty endorsement to a new Progressive Conservative Government.

subsubtopic: PLEA THAT PROVISION OF SURVIVAL SUITS BE MADE MANDATORY
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I would like to draw the attention of the House to the fact that the Ocean Ranger drilling rig sank almost two years ago with the tragic loss of all 84 crew members, in the icy seas off the Newfoundland coast. Unprotected against the cold, no one could expect to survive in those waters.
Rear Admiral Henry Bell, Chairperson of the U.S. Board of Inquiry, said:
There is no question that some of the men would have survived if they had been wearing survival suits. We're not going to re-invent the wheel with this inquiry and prove all over again that survival suits work.
Last night, December 18, the supply tugboat Seaforth JarI sank off the south coast of Newfoundland, in gale force winds and sub-zero temperatures. None of the 11 crew members died, even though they floated in life boats for an hour and a half before being rescued. Each was wearing a survival suit for protection.
The captain and crew of the tugboat Arctic Shiko are to be commended for their speedy rescue under life threatening conditions. However, the Government is to be condemned for its failure to make these life saving survival suits mandatory. While the Government waits for the outcome of the Ocean Ranger inquiry before taking decisive action, other crews may be less fortunate. The time for action has long passed.
December 19, 1983

subsubtopic: CO-OPERATIVE INITIATIVES UNDERTAKEN BY RESIDENTS OF S1CAMOUS, B.C.
speechtext:
Madam Speaker,
I wish to draw the attention of the House of Commons and the federal Government to a most innovative and creative effort being developed by the residents of Sicamous, B.C. The residents of this fine community decided to take the initiative themselves to kick-start the local economic recovery into life, rather than wait for government or outside interests to do it for them. By taking advantage of local human resources, local natural resources, local financial resources, local transportation resources, and a community spirit not found in many communities, a local organization called SWIM was created.
Sicamous Wholesale Industrial Management provides the over-all organization and system for the development of local manufacturing and cottage industries. It assists in developing appropriate community infrastructure not only for the manufacturing of products, but also for their marketing, promotion, and sales. This co-operative effort by the residents of Sicamous, B.C., provides ample evidence that local communities can be part of the solution for a major economic recovery in our country. By skilfully organizing local resources and utilizing peoples' fundamental co-operative inclinations, much can be accomplished.
Positive actions and positive feelings abound in the district as SWIM develops the roots of Canada's recovery process. Not only is SWIM useful in Sicamous, British Columbia, but it can be considered a model for similar communities in all regions of Canada. Thank you, Sicamous, for providing a successful economic development initiative, and a model for the rest of the country.

Madam Speaker, I believe I had occasion to illustrate what 1 meant when I said that the President is now saying things that he had not at least been perceived as saying before. One of the examples I gave was that in the Diet in Tokyo, just a month ago, he came out with a clear statement indicating that he believed that nuclear war could not be won. He believed that we should try to get rid of all nuclear weapons. He also said that he believed that the United States would be flexible in negotiating and that it was looking for an agreement for a lower level of nuclear weapons. These, to my knowledge at least, were statements which I had not seen broadly reported in Canada, and I thought it would be worth while for me to make it clear that we had talked about them during my meeting with the President.

Member would refer to the declaration which came out of that meeting, and to the communique which came out after it, I would think that he would see some very encouraging signs. ministerial level. They agreed that we should review our positions on the MBFR in Vienna and consider whether it would be worth while escalating that to the ministerial level.
The statement was also replete with references to the need for dialogue between East and West and the need not for superiority of the West over East but for a balance in armaments. speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, 1 rise on a point of order to ask for the unanimous consent of the House following consultations with the House Leaders. I refer you to the motion on page 9 of today's Order Paper dealing with parliamentary reform. There is an agreement to that motion from the three Parties under three conditions.
The first condition is the inclusion of a new paragraph after the first paragraph of the motion which would read as follows:
Provided that the Standing Orders shall be further provisionally amended by adding at the end of Standing Order 19:

December 19, 1983
Standing Orders
No Private Members' Business shall be taken up on days appointed for the consideration of business pursuant to Standing Orders 62(5) or 64(4).
This provisional amendment shall cease to have effect as provided for the other provisional Standing Orders in the first paragraph of this Order.
That is the first condition agreed to by the Parties, that the new paragraph 1 just read be added to the motion and included after the first paragraph of the motion standing in my name on page 9 of the Order Paper.
The second condition is that in the report of the Special Committee on Standing Orders, a report that has been printed in Votes and Proceedings for Thursday, December 15, there is printed the new Standing Order 18(5). The condition is that in this new Standing Order 18(5), the brackets that include Private Members' business on Monday, Tuesday, Thursday and Friday be deleted and that the wording be reversed. To be more specific, in the new Standing Order 18(5), when we reach, under Monday, Tuesday and Thursday, what is suggested in the report as "(From five to six o'clock p.m.-Private Members' Business)"-there would be no brackets, and it would read, "Private Members' Business-from five to six o'clock p.m." A bit further in the same Standing Order 18(5), under Friday, it would become, no brackets, "From four to five o'clock p.m.-Private Members' Business". That is the second condition.
The third condition that we have agreed to is to clarify the situation in so far as the third and seventh paragraphs of the first report of the Special Committee are concerned, printed in Votes and Proceedings for Thursday, December 15, 1983. Paragraphs 3 and 7 are not covered by the motion that will be moved today, and which meets with unanimous consent, provided it is amended as 1 have just indicated. Further, I consider that paragraphs 3 and 7 were not covered by the terms of reference of the Committee and are not relevant. Therefore, they will not apply when the motion in my name on the Order Paper today, as amended, is agreed to.
Under those three conditions-and I hope I have been specific enough, and this may be clarified by other House Leaders-it seems there would be unanimous consent to adopt without debate the motion on the Order Paper as it appears at page 9, amended as I have indicated after the first paragraph and in the new Standing Order 18(5), without brackets as I have explained, and paragraphs 3 and 7 of the report not being covered by the motion and not being relevant.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise on a brief point of order flowing from the events of last Friday's Question Period. This point is timely because we are just commencing a new session of Parliament. I raise this point of order not to reflect upon any past decisions of the Chair but to ask you, Mr. Speaker, to consider the direction in which the Chair seems to be going during Question Period. A trend that is rather alarming to me appears to be emerging whereby the Chair exercises editorial decisions as to the nature of the questions that are put to the Minister during the Question Period.
Point of Order-Mr. Nielsen
From this vantage point, Mr. Speaker, it would appear that the Chair has of late been extending the authority afforded to it by this House. In particular, I refer to the fact that one of the occupants of the Chair has begun to exercise the authority of the Chair not only to determine who should be seen by the Chair during the Question Period, not merely to protect and interpret the rules and practices of the House, but to determine the merit of the subject matter addressed in the Question Period. I would refer you to Hansard for Friday, December 16, at page 260, Mr. Speaker. There, following an exchange between the Hon. Member for Saskatoon West (Mr. Hnaty-shyn) and the Minister of Justice (Mr. MacGuigan), the following words attributed to Mr. Deputy Speaker are found:
A short supplementary. The question seems to have been asked on more than one occasion.
I have no difficulty with the fact that Citation 371 of Beauchesne's Fifth Edition points out the following:
The extent to which supplementary questions may be asked is in the discretion of the Speaker.
Indeed, Mr. Speaker, that discretion is exercised almost every day. However, Citation 371 refers to the authority of the Chair to determine the number of supplementary questions to an individual question that may be permitted on any given day.
Citation 371 draws its substance from Erskine May's Nineteenth Edition where British practice with respect to oral questions is outlined. As you are aware, Mr. Speaker, the British practice with respect to oral questions is quite different from our own. At Westminster, a Member gives notice of a given question and supplementary questions are then permitted in order to clarify the Minister's answer or to ensure that all aspects of the original question are addressed. Beauchesne's, at page 134, puts it this way:
Although there may be no debate on an answer, further questions, as may be necessary for the elucidation of the answers that have been given, within due limits, may be addressed to a Minister. The extent to which supplementary questions may be asked is in the discretion of the Speaker. Sir Erskine May, Treatise on the Law, Privileges, Proceedings and Usage of Parliament (19th ed., 1976), pp. 334-5.
The Speaker exercises judgment as to the number of supplementary questions that are necessary in order to ensure a comprehensive response to the Member's original question. There is no suggestion in Erskine May that this judgment should take into account questions which have been asked by a Member on previous occasions or, for that matter, by other Members on previous occasions.
The Chair's comments on Friday with respect to allowing a short supplementary because a question appears to have been asked on more than one occasion seems unusual in the context of the rules governing the Question Period. The Chair appeared to have no concern that the question asked by the Hon. Member for Saskatoon West was out of order; merely, that it may have been soliciting information that had been requested during some other Question Period on some other day.

The difficulty with prohibiting questions on the basis that the information may already be available to the Elouse is that it causes the Chair to place a value judgment on the questions of Hon. Members. Moreover, it is difficult to see how the Chair can determine whether or not new information is being sought before the question has been asked.
In determining whether the Right Hon. Member for Yel-lowhead (Mr. Clark) would be permitted a second supplementary question, Mr. Deputy Speaker again appeared to anticipate the content of a question. Again at page 260, Mr. Deputy Speaker is reported as saying the following:
The Hon. Minister has indicated his difficulty in answering the question. If the Hon. Member-
There were then two interjections. Mr. Deputy Speaker went on to say:

There was then a further interjection.
I would ask you therefore, Mr. Speaker, to consider, not whether the comments of the Chair as recorded in last Friday's Hansard were appropriate at the time but whether this indicates a shift in the thinking of the Chair with respect to the procedures to be followed in future by the Chair and whether or not this is appropriate in the context of the established procedures, both here in Canada and in Great Britain.
While you are considering that point, Mr. Speaker, i would ask you to take the time to reflect on the practices of this House with respect to the order in which Members of this House are recognized during the Question Period. Also, last Friday, the occupant of the chair recognized a member for Her Majesty's Loyal Opposition, the Hon. Member for Well-ington-Dufferin-Simcoe (Mr. Beatty), to ask the first question and two supplementaries. Following those exchanges a member of the New Democratic Party was recognized for three questions. Although it is at the discretion of the Chair to recognize any Member, a practice has evolved, familian to every Member of the House, whereby the first two questioners recognized during a Question Period are representatives of Her Majesty's Loyal Opposition for five questions, in total, and the third questioner is a member of the New Democratic Party for a total a three questions, and sometimes that is split two and one or one and two or some other way; that is their business. The first five are here and the next three are to my left. On Friday last, the Opposition determined that the Hon. Member for Wellington-Dufferin-Simcoe (Mr. Beatty) should be given both of those opening rounds of questions, and the Speaker was informed of our desire in this regard. Instead of following his own opening round of a question and two supplementaries, the Hon. Member for Wellington-Dufferin-Simcoe was required to follow the first question put by a member of the New Democratic Party.
Whether or not the pattern in which Members were recognized for questions last Friday reflects more of Mr. Deputy Speaker's view that it is up to the Chair to determine the
importance of Members' questions, or whether it reflects some other line of thought, 1 would ask you, Mr. Speaker, to consider the implications that this has for the well established practice concerning the order in which Members are recognized in this House during the Question Period.
As 1 stated at the beginning of this point of order, Mr. Speaker, these two matters indicate, in my view, a disturbing trend in the exercise of the authority of the Chair and I would ask you to consider the matter and take whatever action you deem to be necessary.
I suggest, Mr. Speaker, that you might want to consider this matter over tomorrow and perhaps come back to the House on Wednesday-indeed, I would not be in the least bit disturbed or put out if you wanted to take the whole of the Christmas recess to consider the matter.

The question that I would like to raise relates to the matter of granting charitable status to charitable organizations under this legislation, and particularly the need to place in the statute a definition to handle the problem of defining charitable organizations. I would like to take a few minutes to present a situation to the Government and ask the Minister for his interpretation of the problem and to tell us what action the Government intends to take to resolve the problem.
To illustrate the problem 1 would like to compare two charitable organizations in the country. The first organization is the B.C. section of the Canadian Mental Health Association. This was raised in the House by the Hon. Member for Waterloo on November 2, 1983. He pointed out that the Department of National Revenue had been involved in encouraging the B.C. section of the Canadian Mental Health Association to change its constitution, to remove an objectionable section in the statement of purpose which is to advocate and lobby for improvement and integration of treatment rehabilitation services for persons who become handicapped or disabled by emotional disorders. The key point is that the function of the group was to represent the interests of handicapped persons in this country by educating and providing information, especially in some of the technical areas, to legislators. That is an extremely important function if in fact the legislature is going to assist in it. There does seem to be a need for some change. The best change may come through a definition placed in the legislation that would accommodate
Income Tax Act
that kind of activity for an organization which, beyond any shadow of a doubt, is truly charitable in nature.
The other organization which I think it would pay for the Minister to peruse in his comparison when he is looking for an appropriate definition is the Fraser Institute. The Fraser Institute is licensed as an organization with charitable status under the Income Tax Act. It represents a vey small, privileged right wing group in our society. Its unstated purpose in 1974 was to focus on efforts to get rid of the NDP Government in British Columbia. Its activities involved providing advice and active policy direction to the Social Credit Government in B.C. It is probably one of the most right wing and reactionary groups in North America. The executive director of the Fraser Institute publicly bragged of that fact.
I would like to read into the record a small analysis of Richard Gwynn. In speaking of Michael Walker he states: "He founded the Fraser Institute in 1974 after a bunch of B.C. businessmen came up with the money, not so much because they cared about his ideas, but they cared deeply about getting rid of New Democrat Premier, Dave Barrett, and getting him out of office." That is Richard Gwynn's analysis of the charitable nature of that organization. When you compare it to organization like the Mental Health Association, things start to get a little bit fuzzy regarding how the Department is handling the question of defining charitable organizations.
1 would like to point out that one of the policy decisions which the Fraser Institute has come up with is to abolish minimum wage. Its idea is that you can hire four handicapped people at $1 an hour instead of one person at S3.65, which would presumably give some benefit to the economy. It advocates the abolition of rent controls. It is opposed to equal pay for equal work for men and women. In one of its publications it states that to discriminate in a democratic society is a right. This organization has had charitable status in this country since 1974 through a failure by the Government to provide an adequate definition in its legislation of what in fact a charitable organization is. It is extremely ironic when an organization such as the B.C. branch of the Canadian Mental Health Association has to be hauled up and chastised when an organization as blatant as this can continue to function. The board of directors of the Fraser Institute represents such stalwart and well represented groups as B.C. Packers, The Royal Bank of Canada, The Bank of Commerce, IBM of Canada and Gen-star. I would say that that group certainly is not one of the key demanders of charity in this country.
In short, Mr. Chairman, the Fraser Institute is not a charitable organization. It is an active political organization giving policy advice and direction to one of the most right wing governments and right wing politicians in Canada. It is not illegal in Canada to play the role of social and economic dinosaur, but it is illegal for the Fraser Institute to have charitable status, and it is immoral for the Government to permit this type of antisocial and anti-people propaganda to be developed and disseminated with the support of public funds.
I would like to use one more example, Mr. Chairman, to show that the Fraser Institute is a political organization

If you follow the train of logic of the NDP, it is urging a Minister of the Crown to use the Income Tax Act to cut into the very basic principle of freedom of speech, which is very important to the lifeblood of universities. I am hoping that the Minister can reassure the House that he is not being trapped into using provisions in the Income Tax Act to deny Canadians the principle of freedom of speech. Can I have that assurance from the Minister?

Mr. Chairman, I have listened to the discussion with some interest. The Hon. Member opposite is right in identifying the Income Tax Act as the legislation which provides the Government with the opportunity to designate certain charitable entities as exempt from the normal tax which would otherwise be levied.
However, the implementation of that legislation, the regulations under which the exemption is provided to any specific institution or organization, is entirely within the purview of the Department of National Revenue. The Department of National Revenue, in assessing the qualifications and merits of an organization for the exemption which it seeks, is based on case law, based on precedent, based on traditions that are well established in our country. It would be quite inappropriate for me to comment on the specific instance that the Hon. Member opposite has raised. I would suggest to him that if he has some specific misgiving about any particular organization or entity which has received, does now receive or may in the future receive some exemption, he would do well to address himself to the Minister of National Revenue and make his views known to him.

Mr. Chairman, I do not want this to slip by because the case law the Minister refers to is absolutely right. The courts have grappled with the question of what is a charitable organization and what is a political organization. One of the definitions is that a political organization involved with political activity is, by definition, excluded from being a charity.
I have asked the Minister to review these two cases, one raised by a member of the Conservative Party and the other raised by myself, because one way out of this particular dilemma is for the federal Government to place an appropriate
December 19, 1983

clause within the Income Tax Act that defines what a charity is so we are not in a situation in which we find ourselves now.
With respect to the points raised by the previous speaker, this is not an attempt to curtail free speech. As a matter of fact, I mentioned before that if an organization wanted to perform the role of a social and economic dinosaur and disseminate propaganda of that nature, it is absolutely not illegal to do that in Canada. However, it is really immoral to do it through any method of public financing. Otherwise, we should finance every group, and I am sure the Hon. Member does not accept that proposition.
1 recognize the split responsibilities with the Minister of National Revenue who was left with the dilemma of evaluating the organization, but certainly the Minister responsible for the Income Tax Act must familiarize himself with it, come to some kind of conclusion with regard to these problems, and then provide us with an amendment which would remove this type of anomaly in the income tax legislation.

Mr. Chairman, again I have listened with interest to the comments of the Hon. Member opposite. There is a body of case law available to the Hon. Member to guide him in his thinking about the ways in which the Department of National Revenue adjudicates these often difficult questions of deciding what entity should qualify for the tax exemption which the Hon. Member has raised. The subject is one which the Hon. Member opposite will know is under consideration at all times by the Government. It is an evolving and dynamic question as is implied by the fact that case law and precedent are largely relied upon to provide guidance in applications of this sort.
To move toward some precise definition and to attempt to draft some very precise definition of what an institution must be to qualify for tax exemption status would be to impose a straitjacket, which I think all Members would find quite unsatisfactory in a very short period. The nature of our society changes and evolves and new institutions come forward to address new issues which emerge in our society. I would have thought that it is simply beyond the wit of any of us to devise a definition of such precision that it would be durable over a prolonged period. It is for that reason, basically, that the Department of National Revenue has relied upon precedents and case law as the guiding lights in this issue.
I would only add to what I said to the Hon. Member opposite that, without reference to the specific entities that he raised, we on the government side are keeping this issue under review and the question of definition of charitable organizations is never far from our minds.

Mr. Chairman, I had not intended to question the Minister on this issue until he made his statements in the last few moments. However, 1 do so because some of us have been very concerned for a long time about the imprecision in the definition regarding charitable organizations under the Act and also about the attempts that have been made in the past by the Department of National Revenue to
Income Tax Act
superimpose itself on the various organizations throughout the country.
The Hon. Minister may remember that the Honourable Joseph Guay, now a Senator in the other place, when he was Minister of National Revenue indeed began to apply a very precise definition to what a charitable organization was, using, as he said, the definition that exists at the present time. What ensued was a complete uproar among charitable organizations, certainly with members of the Opposition Party which I represent and with the House as a whole. It got to the point where the Government and the Department of National Revenue were forced to change the straitjacket that they were trying to impose on charitable organizations, including churches. For instance, at that point it began to look as though a minister or a priest of a church who preached on any subject that could be termed political in any way would stand in jeopardy of losing his charitable number.
I raise this question because the Minister has now indicated that there is an ongoing review. My understanding at that time was that the Department would withdraw any kind of imposition or restriction of the definition that was then being applied and that at some time it would come back with a definition which we in the House could debate. We have heard nothing more since that time. Is there anything going on behind the scenes that would again arouse the concerns of the 47,000 charitable institutions across this country?

Mr. Chairman, we have no intention of attempting to provide, as it were, a straitjacket definition which would in some way constrain the activities of voluntary organizations and charitable activities across the country. Indeed, I listened with interest to the Hon. Member and find myself in agreement with very much of what she said. If she inferred from what I said earlier that I had in mind that we were, as a government, going to come forward shortly with some specific definition of a very precise order, then I was unclear in what I intended to say. To the contrary, I very much have in mind the general considerations which she has brought forward in the sense that society changes and issues emerge that were not foreseen in earlier decades. I suppose one could take any example, but the environment might be an example to illustrate the point. I am old enough to remember three decades ago when environmental issues were not of prime concern. Indeed, it lacked any organization aside from one or two honourable exceptions. These acted as advocates for the concern of those who wanted to see our environment afforded better protection. Gradually such organizations have emerged. They have acquired the tax exempt status which enables them to pursue their laudable activities. I think we are talking about a dynamic area which is kept under constant review by the Department of National Revenue. I would agree with the Hon. Member opposite that this is a question which we would do well to keep under constant examination as our society evolves.

December 19, 1983
Income Tax Act

1 have one short supplementary, Mr. Chairman. The reason there was such concern at the time this issue was raised by the former Minister of National Revenue was that charitable organizations felt there was no protection within the present definition from any government of the day moving against them. What they have been asking ever since is that government, the charitable organizations and the vast body of volunteers across the country come together to discuss what could be a more reasonable definition, a more precise definition, which at the same time does not make them vulnerable to any kind of move that an incumbant government may try to make against them.
Is this being considered? Certainly it has been advocated by the national voluntary coalition at the present time, not that the Government impose itself unilaterally, but that something be done by means of a reference to a parliamentary committee where there could be representations made and where all Parties in Parliament would be able to provide some input to the Government so that there would be no danger to the voluntary organizations in the country of suddenly finding they were being cut off from the charitable status that they now enjoy.

Mr. Chairman, again I find myself in broad agreement with the purposes behind the Hon. Member's intervention. It is certainly not our wish to jeopardize in some way the activities of bona fide charitable organizations. On the contrary, the Hon. Member opposite may recall that in the recent Speech from the Throne the Government stated its determined support for the activities of voluntary organizations, an element in our society which has perhaps not always received the recognition that it deserves. I have myself a real conviction that we will see in the time ahead voluntary organizations play a greater role in our society. It is not our intention to engage in any restriction on the legal, as it were, or the justifiable activities of those institutions receiving exemption from taxation. We have the matter under consideration. I have noted what the Hon. Member said. I am sure she will afford us further opportunity to have the benefit of her contributions in the future.

Mr. Chairman, there have been organizations that have been, and I would use the term, harassed as to whether or not they have been involved in political activity, and those groups have been threatened by the Department of losing their status. There are other organizations, and 1 would use the example of environmental groups which have been denied status. Ultimately, the concern and worry at each step of the game is whether or not the organizations have political objectives. Do they, in fact, wish to change laws in the country or influence legislators or politicians? Do they dessiminate and produce propaganda? These are the kinds of definitions on which the courts have been falling back. When they have a very hard question, such as whether an organization is charitable, they have used a blanket interpretation that if an organization has political objectives, then it is not a charitable
organization. I would say that probably one of the most difficult situations with which the Minister has to come to grips is with an organization, about which there is no doubt in the minds of anyone in the House that it is a charitable organization providing very worthy support for people across the country, yet there is another organization which, in the minds of tens if not hundreds of thousands of Canadians, is totally political in nature but which qualifies for charitable status. The Department has again, using the court-based rulings, denied access to quite a number of groups that have applied for charitable status under the same terms and conditions as the Fraser Institute. You cannot have it both ways. We have to have at least the assurance of the Minister, either that we may find something in the statute that would allow for an appeal to an independent group from the Department that it can do without some horrendous expense and difficulty, or else that we will move to allow some kind of definition in the legislation that would broaden the situation for people and maybe not put them under such close interpretation of legal statements by the bureaucracy.
I would like the Minister to give us an indication what is involved in this review that he has going on right now. Is he reviewing what the Fraser Institute and other charitable organizations are doing? Is he reviewing the situation with a possibility of creating a statutory definition of a charitable organization or possibly putting in an appeal process for those who have been denied and harassed? It is a very difficult situation when you get a call from National Revenue suggesting that your organization is becoming involved politically and may lose its tax number or that the organization has been denied the right to a tax number. Essentially, what happens is that there is a withdrawal from a very important area, such as education of legislators and making presentations on an organization's objectives and points to governments. I suggest that this is a very important function for advocacy groups. The Minister should be looking at some method of allowing that to go forward.

Mr. Chairman, I believe the Hon. Member opposite has raised two broad areas of concern. One relates to the definition or qualification of specific entities. It is not my purpose today to comment on the institutions he has named, but rather merely to say, as I mentioned earlier, that we believe for our part that, generally speaking, the public is best served in this instance by a procedure that is flexible, which does take account of the changing character of the Canadian society and which, through precedent, case law, enables the qualifications of applicants to be tested and examined.
I have taken note of the intervention of the Hon. Member and indeed the intervention of the Hon. Member for Kingston and the Islands on the question. We will bear their points very much in mind.
With regard to the second point, the question of an appeal procedure of some sort, that is one which requires some examination. In the time ahead I hope we will have the opportunity to look more closely at the possibility of the

provision of some appeal procedure. I thank the Hon. Member for his contribution.

Mr. Chairman, this particular series of revisions is a new concept in the Income Tax Act that gives those persons who invest in the securities of some 1,100 or 1,150 listed companies in Canada the right to have their securities registered in what is called an indexed security fund or plan. These securities are then treated on the basis that the income or dividends from the securities are paid out to the holder in

December 19, 1983
Income Tax Act
the ordinary course and receive the dividend tax credits and the like, but from then on, the gain is indexed and the annual gain on the portfolio is treated as an indexed gain, and taxes therefore are only paid on the real gain as opposed to the inflationary gain. Indeed, only 25 per cent of the real gain is brought into tax each year.
The same applies, of course, for losses. If there is a loss on the security, the loss can be written off. Through the provision of this particular fund or plan, the loss can be written off in full and not only as against security income but as against any income.
The plan enables those who invest in the stock market to have their capital gains indexed and their capital losses totally deductible, on a 50 per cent basis, of course, from their other income. It treats those who are in the preferred position of having purchased Canadian securities through a Canadian stock exchange in a listed Canadian company the right to pay only capital gains tax on real gains and it gives them the right to deduct all of their losses. In our view, it is pretty unfair to allow one group of investors to have a benefit of this nature whereas other investors receive no such benefit.
This does not mean that we are opposed to indexing of capital gains tax, because we are not. Indeed, we would go so far as to say that the capital gains tax should be completely abolished. However, to allow those who buy the securities of large corporations the right to have their gains indexed and to say to those who invest in small or private business that is not listed on the stock exchange or those who buy farms or small businesses that they should pay full capital gains tax on all of the gain including the inflationary gain and that they should only be able to deduct their capital losses from other income at the rate of $2,000 a year is discrimination of the worst order. Indeed, it is counterproductive and is harmful to Canada. If we are going to do what is contemplated in these particular sections, then we should do it for all.
I would ask the Minister how he can justify to his constituents who have small businesses that they should not be able to have indexation on the value of their small businesses and that they should not be able to write their entire loss off against their other income if they suffer a loss.

Mr. Chairman, I have listened with attention to the Hon. Member's observations. I have noted with interest his support for the measure we are now discussing, which is the ISIP program. I take it that his principal thesis is that in offering support for ISIP, he would want to see the same thing being extended to the valuation of other assets and to the impact of capital gains and how those capital gains are taxed on other assets.
I am sure that the Hon. Member opposite appreciates that at the present time the Government is reviewing other areas of investment which are affected by inflation. We have under review many of the points that he has offered us today. The challenge in those areas, however, is rather more difficult than it has proven to be in the case of Canadian equity traded on our stock markets. On commonly traded shares, of course, there is a ready method of valuation. That method is available on a daily, monthly or annual basis. It provides a ready measurement of capital gains and therefore a ready way for those capital gains to be taxed.
December 19, 1983

Our initiative in this area is really only the first of what I hope will be other initiatives to provide Canadians some protection against the inflationary impact on the valuation of their assets and on assets other than Canadian common shares. However, in this instance, we moved because we could move quickly. We moved first by consulting with those in the industry and with the financial institutions about the ways in which such a program could be implemented. We sought the advice of the Investment Dealers Association, we sought the advice of stock exchanges across Canada and we sought the advice of financial institutions generally. We invited a private sector committee to examine the proposition and report back after consultations throughout the business community with recommendations on how we might move to immunize the capital gains on common shares from normal inflation.
In reviewing the possible extension of that thinking on other forms of assets and referring to the possible extension of this approach to inflationary increases in the value of assets to the sale of shares of private companies, the Lortie Commission pointed out that this suggestion had been examined. It concluded that such adjustments could not feasibly be carried out within the RSIP-which is to say, the 1SIP-or any similar plan, but any gain arising on the disposition of a share of a private company should be subject to tax only when actually realized. The report said that it is inappropriate to include in RSIPs assets such as the shares of private companies which cannot be readily valued and which have limited liquidity. In any event, the report pointed out, there are complications in any system of indexing the cost of shares of private companies, such complications relating to the deductibility of interest on loans taken out to acquire such shares.
There is a dual difficulty in the valuation of assets including the sale of shares of private companies and also, of course, including such assets as a farm or other forms of private property. That difficulty has not deterred us from examining ways in which that same protection from inflation might be extended to other areas.
Nevertheless, while that intention is there to examine other ways in which such protection could be offered, the Government has sought parallel ways in which small business could benefit from tax changes. We have a lower corporate tax rate for small business, small business bonds are available, there is an exemption on sales tax and there is a full offset of capital losses on private company shares and obligations, which can only be of assistance to small business.
I could draw the attention of the committee to other forms of assistance available to small business but I only want to add that the broad question which the Hon. Member opposite has raised is one of common concern. We share his interest in an extension of that sheltering or protection or immunization from the impacts of inflation on the value of capital assets in the way he has described. However, it is not an area where it is easy to take quick measures to bring forward the benefits that he and I both seek.
Income Tax Act
Mr. Speaker, 1 have a series of questions for the Minister. Is the 1S1P initiative in this tax Bill the major initiative in the whole Bill?

No, Mr. Chairman, the IS IP is one of the major measures in the Bill, but there are a number of measures which arose from the commitment of the Government to promote economic recovery in Canada.
The Hon. Member will recall that in the budget two ranges of measures were offered: a short term and an immediate public investment to promote jobs and to help create the infrastructure necessary for further economic expansion but, in parallel, measures to promote the creation of employment and extension in the private sector. The ISIP measure should be seen as part of that second emphasis in the April Budget and in the tax measures now before us.
It would be misleading for me to say that ISIP represents the major element in the tax measures; on the contrary. For example, among the recovery incentives the investment tax credit proposals play a major part. Hon. Members will be aware of the incentives available for additional R and D activity, an area that is of concern to Canadians generally. We have also offered better treatment for tax losses by extending tax carryforwards and tax carrybacks to address, in part, the concern that the Hon. Member opposite and 1 share about liquidity problems that face some Canadian corporations and measures to increase the cash flow of those corporations.
On a personal level with regard to individual Canadians, we have increased the rate of the employment expense deduction and we have increased the child tax credit as measures which we hope respond to the concerns of lower income Canadians, especially in a time of economic recession.

speechtext:

Member for Calgary West again. 1 would ask the Hon. Member has made that point, if the Hon. Member for Bow River were agreeable, I would change the Chair's recognition and recognize the Hon.

December 19, 1983

Member for Calgary West until such time as I look at the subject on a procedural basis. Is that agreed?
Yes, Mr. Chairman.

Thank you, Mr. Chairman, and I thank the Hon. Member for Bow River. If we could avoid filibusters it would be helpful because we might have to respond in kind.
The Minister has told us that this is not the major measure, but it is major. He has told us that it is designed to help the economic recovery. Could the Minister share with the House an estimate of how many dollars the Government expects to be invested in ISIPs within a year or five years or perhaps a longer period? How much money does he think will go into ISIPs? What is the Government's projection?

Mr. Chairman, 1 cannot offer the Hon. Member the number that he seeks off the top of my head. I would point out that the amount of net capital gains on shares in 1980 was about $2.9 billion but that, of course, fluctuates from year to year and is dependent in part on the inflation rate. In five years we expect all individuals to hold most, if not all, of their common shares through ISIP so as to obtain that protection from the inflationary impact on that capital gains which otherwise common shares would attract.

Mr. Chairman, could I ask the Minister if the tax system intends to treat differently a dollar which is invested in a new stock issue, an offering on behalf of a company to raise capital, or if I choose to buy some existing stock from someone who already holds it? If 1 put those two situations into the ISIP, would 1 be treated any differently within the tax system?
No, Mr. Chairman, there would be no difference accorded to either newly issued shares or to shares currently traded on the exchanges.

Does the Minister see a difference for the economy in a rollover situation or in the purchase of new shares? Does one or the other help the economy more or less? And could he explain to us which one he thinks helps the economy the most?

We consulted, as I noted earlier, with the private sector and with the Investment Dealers Association and the stock exchanges, amongst others, across Canada, on this and related questions. It is our view, and the view of those who are active in the industry, that there will be no difference.
1 sense the Hon. Member opposite-without wishing to put words in his mouth-feels there may be some tendency on the part of the market to place an emphasis either on newly issued shares or on shares currently traded. That is not our impression and it is not our expectation. We would assume that the investor will seek his capital gains protection on both existing shares and on new shares.

Mr. Chairman, that answer is a bit confusing. The question was: if someone sitting over here on my left has a million dollars to invest, and very Canadian, does it help the economy more if he invests in a new share offering or if he simply invests in a rollover? We can make the assumption that a new share offering is being offered by a company because it needs capital to modernize, to bring in new technology, to expand its sales force, to do something with new capital. That is what a new share offering is all about. I am wondering whether or not the Minister is trying to tell me there is really no difference between buying a rollover in a rollover situation, and putting money into a new share offering, in its impact on jobs.
No, Mr. Chairman. I was attempting to tell the Hon. Member opposite that the ISIP treats new share issues and existing shares in the same way.

What we are intending here, in this legislation, is to give some kind of tax break to people who roll things over. Can the Minister tell me whether there is any necessity-let us say a billion dollars comes into it-that one single job be created in the economy in return for the tax treatment?

Mr. Chairman, the point I wanted to make, and I evidently have not made it clearly, is that we are blind, as it were, to the question of whether new shares or existing shares are being traded. The exemption from the inflationary part of capital gains tax is treated exactly the same in the case of both shares. It is our view that any other distinction-if we attempted to make any distinction-between old and new issues, would lead to complexities not only in the legislation but in the administration of the program.
We also, in equity, feel that current holders of shares need an inflation offset as much as new share investors. I do not know whether the Hon. Member opposite is advocating a system whereby only new shares would be exempted from capital gains-the inflationary element of capital gains-for a certain period. If that is what he is advocating, I do not think I could agree with him. 1 would not want to support such an approach. Obviously, the one immediate impact of any such move would be to attract money away from existing investments into new share issues, and I cannot see that that would be of any benefit to our economy generally.

One of the fears we have on this side is that indeed money may be pulled out of small business. An equity venture capital fund is not protected against inflation necessarily, either by putting it into existing stock on a rollover basis or not doing so. It seems to me that the Canadian economy needs more venture capital. Everything one reads suggest we need venture capital. Why is the Government at this particular period in our history encouraging traders, rollovers, instead of money being put into venture capital? Why is the Government making this public policy choice?

Mr. Chairman, the Hon. Member opposite may be making rather more difficulty over the listing of shares than I think perhaps is justified. However, bearing in mind his
December 19, 1983

admonition to be brief and not to engage in what he rather unkindly described as "filibustering", I will only say to him that there is a whole range, as I think he knows so well, of other measures, not only in the tax Bill now before us but in existing Government legislation, which is intended to promote the growth of small business. I do not believe he and I would have any disagreement on the role played by small business and the role played by the entrepreneur in our economy. I mentioned earlier the lower tax rate available for small business. I mentioned the programs of small business loans and assistance available to small businesses to promote their activities. I think what we see here is a program which takes into account the nature of the Canadian equity markets, parallel to taking into account the particular needs of small business.
One of the common things on the stock market is that people sell short. That is one of the ways they take a risk. What happens within an IS1P? Can people sell short?

I am sorry, Mr. Chairman. I wonder whether the Hon. Member would mind repeating his question.
I did not hear all of it.

One of the things which happens in the stock market is that traders sell short. They make a gain sometimes and they have a loss at other times. Are those kinds of gains and losses included within ISIP?

Yes, Mr. Chairman, those gains or losses are included under ISIP. There are special rules for call and put options. Perhaps the Hon. Member wants to be more specific about his concerns. I am not sure I follow exactly what it is he is concerned about.

It seems to me we are setting up a situation here, Mr. Chairman, where a taxpayer in this country can sell something he does not own. If he loses money on it, the taxpayers will pick up part of it. If he gains money on it, they will only pick up the portion of the share they would ordinarily be entitled to. Is that part of the purpose of the ISIP legislation?

I am not sure of the purport of the Hon. Member's reasoning, Mr. Chairman. It may be that he is advocating a fundamental change in the nature of marginal trading or in our equity system in Canada. If he is not advocating that, I do not see how he can single out certain activities or benefits under the ISIP program to the exclusion of others. I feel one would want to take the market as it operates today, accept it as it operates today, apply the ISIP program to the total activities of the market, and not single out within that total activity certain practices which would be exempted from the benefits of the ISIP program.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I would like to go back just a bit because the Member has stepped back in his question to an earlier comment he made and I would like to do the same. He raised the question of whether ISIP could potentially draw money out of the small business sector, for example, into common shares which would perhaps, by definition, favour larger companies, certainly the more established ones.
The question is a good one but it comes at the problem from a slightly wrong angle. I suggest to the Hon. Member that the over-all problem we are facing in the business community today is an overload of debt, with a great deal of non-productive interest payments going out as opposed to dividend payments or rewards for risk. The Government would like to shift capital not from small business to big business, not from unlisted companies to listed companies, and not from one activity to another, but within one area. We would like to help those companies with listed common shares through this plan to get off the debt route a little bit and get more reliance on equity.
In the budget announced last April there were other measures which will help small business, farmers and unlisted companies to go through the same exercise. For example, we are allowing people to write off their debts further into the past and into the future. That will erase the impact of high interest rates as we have just experienced them, give them a bit of money through the tax system and, hopefully, allow them to diminish their debt in that fashion. Equally we have incentives in the share purchase plan.
The Hon. Member asked a reasonable question, whether we would be distorting the market, but I ask him to consider the other instruments here as well and not just this one. 1 also point out that the general creation of this kind of strength in the business community has gone to the jobs he is referring to. Clearly, if a business has money to spend for expansion, it will create new jobs. If a business has profits, it can make a decision about whether it will plow those profits back into its operation or distribute them to its shareholders. It does not have that kind of decision when it is faced with debt. Automatically it must pay the debt and the interest.
I believe the creation of a stronger equity base for our businesses through this measure, but also through the others, is going to help them expand. Quite frankly, I thought the statement made in the April Budget along this line was quite a good one. It was quite a clear analysis of the problem that our

December 19, 1983
Income Tax Act
business community faces. 1 must say, with all respect, that I differ with my friends in the NDP who have tended to call this a measure for the rich and comfortable.
That is exactly what it is.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: Quite frankly, if a business has money to expand, it is going to expand and not sit still. It is going to create jobs and new activity for itself and its suppliers through its equity and profits. Again I repeat to the Hon. Member that businesses do not have that option when they are dealing with debt. They must pay their lenders. The Hon. Member asked this question quite sincerely, and 1 think he has asked the right question and 1 congratulate him for it.

If the Minister accepts the statement made by his Parliamentary Secretary that the purpose is to reduce company debt, would the Government accept the proposition that any new share offering put out in the public domain for the reduction of debt be put in ISIP and all other things excluded? In that way you target specifically on what the Parliamentary Secretary tells us is the problem. You can do it but you cannot have that necessary new money competing with rollovers because rollovers are nine times out of ten more attractive. They are less risk. If you really want to help the Canadian economy and reduce debt, as you said, then target it.
Will the Government conform with an amendment of that kind, which would target the money on the problem, that is the reduction of debt?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, again it is a key question and I congratulate the Hon. Member for zeroing in on this topic. The problem is, how would he deal with a businessman like me, for example?
God only knows.

But you think you should pay capital gains taxes on inflation, do you not?

-which I could use to determine whether we had a loss or gain, it would be almost impossible to measure the goodwill factor in my business, even though I might claim it is there. So I ask the Hon. Member to consider that difficulty and remember that when pursuing this search for equity he could make life much, much worse for my company.
I would much rather have other ways besides ISIP to overcome my equity problem. I would like to have some of the flexibility in the tax system that the carry-back and carry-forward provisions provide. I would like to have access to the
small business loan and small business rate. Those things are much more valuable to me than an ISIP, which will automatically involve complicated calculations, and they are not going to give the real value the Hon. Member I am sure is sincerely asking to have. I think that there are entirely different problems in small unlisted businesses which we can address in other ways to get the same result, namely more equity and less debt. Certainly using the flexibility of the tax system has done that, especially on the question of writing off losses.

Mr. Chairman, I want to deal with this topic from an agricultural point of view. 1 was interested when the Minister said that one of the objectives of this legislation is to tax only when the profits are actually realized. I suggest that the Government's priority in this particular phase is incorrect. One of the greatest producers of wealth in this land is the farmer. Yet the farmer is the one who is taking one of the worst beatings on capital gains taxes of anyone in the country. For example, land is sold for many reasons. It might be sold for a subdivision, which will realize very large sums of money. If you are close to a city, that is a possibility. I am going to speak now about land that is 30 or 50 miles away from a major city to show how unfair the present system is to those farmers who are producing. I am talking about land that was settled by a man, his wife and family about 50 years ago. The children of that family have now passed away or gone to other places, except for one son. That son still farms the home land. He is not married and has no children. He wants to sell that land now to a nephew. Under the Act an uncle is not included in the family rollover. 1 think that is unfair, but that is the way the Act is. The value of that land becomes the question. The nephew is anxious to take the land, but not at an inflated value which the land will never pay back. He had the manager of a Canadian Imperial Bank of Commerce check the land to ascertain how long it would take the production of that land to pay back the purchase price. The bank manager said that that land would pay back its capital value in seven or ten years at $200 an acre. The Department of National Revenue people say that the going price of that land is in the area of $500 an acre. That is inflated not only by inflation by also by land that is going to be used for other purposes than agriculture. It is most unfair to say to this man, "You are going to have to pay $500 an acre" when that land will never produce enough to pay that back to the farmer.
That is the point which 1 am trying to make today. Unless the land is able to produce enough to pay back the price, then a reasonable purchaser is not going to buy it. You buy a business with the understanding that the production from that business will eventually pay off that purchase price. That is impossible under these conditions. If the nephew buys the land at $500 an acre, he is buying land that will never pay for itself. If he buys it at $200 an acre, which is the value put on it by the bank manager, then it will pay for itself over a reasonable length of time. I would like to ask the Minister whether it is fair to say to our producers, "You are going to be stuck with
December 19, 1983

this inflated value but the bond holders are not going to be stuck with the inflated value"? Surely the Government realizes that unless that land is going to produce enough to pay back the purchase price there is something wrong with the tax.
Is the Minister prepared to look at this particular thing in regard to the Department of National Revenue? 1 see that the Minister of National Revenue is here even though he is not listening. He should be listening. The Department of National Revenue is putting an unfair burden on those who want to buy land when they give it an inflated value of $500 when that land will never produce enough to pay back that purchase price. Are the Minister and the Government prepared to look at this particular problem? After all, the production from our farm lands is probably the most important thing in our country today.

Mr. Chairman, I listened with interest, as always, to the Member opposite, especially when he discusses the agricultural sector with which he is so familiar. The broad question he raises is one of interest to us. We have been reviewing some of the elements he has discussed, however briefly, today. We will continue to bear his concerns in mind.
However, in relating the IS1P proposal to the situation of farmers I would like to offer him a few comments. He began his statement by saying that gains under the ISIP program would only be taxed on the sale of the assets. That is not in fact the case. The tax is levied on an annual basis. I would like to give the Hon. Member opposite an illustration of what I have in mind in the case of ISIP. If there were a capital gain of $60 in the course of a year, in the current year the investor would have to report one-quarter of that, or $15. The taxable portion of that is one-half, that is, $7.50. The tax rate on that taxable portion is 50 per cent. Therefore, the tax payable would be $3.75. I offer the Member that illustration merely to point out to him that in fact under the ISIP program the tax is levied annually, unlike in the case of the sale of farm land where capital gain on the land is not taxed until the sale itself. It is not taxed on an annual basis but rather when the land is sold.
The difficulty with assets other than common stock arises from the difficulty of evaluating the asset.
Nonsense, absolute nonsense.
Perhaps the Hon. Member has some suggestions about-
You do not have to value the assets.

-how it is feasible to value annually other forms of assets, including, in his instance, farm land. The second area which gives some difficulty is that under the ISIP program interest paid on money borrowed for investment in common shares is non-deductible. The same would apply if we were to try to extend this program to other forms of assets, including farm land. If money had been borrowed to purchase the farm land the interest would not be deductible. 1 think the Member-
Income Tax Act
Why is interest not deductible?

-opposite might have some problem with that. The Member opposite will also be aware that in the case of farm land sold to children no tax is attracted.
The final point that the Member made was something about benefiting bond holders under ISIP. Perhaps I did not quite understand his point. The ISIP program does not extend to bonds but rather to equity investment in common shares.

I would like to continue briefly. 1 want to make sure the Government is going to give this problem consideration. It is one of the major problems facing the farmers of Canada today, not only in the west, but all over Canada. I would compare it with the pensions of Members of the House.
1 do not think I will ever get mine, but when those Members who have served a number of years in this House start getting their pension, they will pay income tax on the pension as they receive it year by year. They will not have to pay on the whole pension. That is the part which a farmer finds very unfair. He works 40 years to build up his farm. That is the only pension he has. Then he sells his farm, as this uncle is now wanting to do. He wants to retire. All the wealth he has in the world is in that farm. When he sells that he has nothing left. If he sells that farm, he is going to be taxed on the whole thing the same year he sells it. He will have half of whatever amount of money he receives calculated in his income tax. That will bring it down to a point where he is not able to sell the land because he cannot live on that amount. He still has a number of years to live. It is unfair when one sees others who are building up a pension the way Members of the House of Commons do and compares them with the way farmers or some businesses do it.
1 want to suggest that if we are going to have capital gains-which I do not believe is necessary-it could be more equitable if we allowed the farmer to spread the payment over a number of years. This would be comparable to what other Canadians do, because the present system certainly is not fair.
My second point concerns the rollover from father to son. There are also cases of a rollover from uncle to nephew. Since the farmer may not have any children, the rollover would go to a nephew, who also has some right to the land since his father was part of the family which originally settled that land. Perhaps consideration should be given to including the relatives such as uncles and aunts in these rollover provisions.
My other point concerns valuation. I hope that the Government will accept the fact that the valuation of the land should be based upon what that land can produce, particularly when it is being sold and used as agricultural land. I realize that complications can arise with respect to subdivisions on land that is close to cities, but in cases of strictly agricultural land with no thought of using it for anything but agricultural, the value should be based on what that land would produce in wheat, oats, barley or cattle.
If this were done, the inflated value would be eliminated. If the Government would do as the Hon. Minister of Agriculture

December 19, 1983
Income Tax Act
suggested, and indeed as the Right Hon. Prime Minister suggested in the last election, that is, raised that valuation day by two or three years, it would make a world of difference to how Canadian farmers would look upon this valuation. Certainly it is completely unfair to put a value on land which it never will be able to repay. 1 want to emphasize that point over and over because of the unfairness to farmers who must buy land at an inflated value knowing that they will never be able to pay back that value plus the interest from the production of that land. 1 wish the Hon. Minister, who I know is sincere, would consider some of these points, because they are vitally important to the producers of this country.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I have indicated to the Minister that I would like to make a couple of comments on this because my friend and I have had many discussions about this issue. 1 would also refer him to the very fruitful discussions that took place in the Finance Committee a year ago on this topic precisely. I think it is only fair that I should mention that four of our Members from southwestern Ontario have been very determined on this issue. They are the Member for Kent, the Member for Lambton-Middlesex, the Member for Essex-Kent, and the Member for London-Middlesex. Those four Members have been very concerned about this issue precisely.
1 am not quite clear about how we can deal with this issue without abolishing capital gains on farm land altogether. I do not think that that would be a particularly fair treatment of farm land. I must confess that to the Hon. Member. I know that in his area there would not be too much difficulty in definining what is a farm and what is not a farm, but in the area that my friend from Mississauga South and I come from, there would be tremendous difficulty defining what is and what is not farmland. It would be difficult to determine if people were legitimately involved in farming on any given piece of land or whether it was being held simply for its real estate value or future industrial use or residential development. We really get into some difficulty in the tax system in these growth areas around cities. With respect to these categories, I believe we would begin to distort the real estate market because we would be pulling people into real estate speculation because of the absence of the capital gains tax. That would be a real problem. I saw the Hon. Member nod his head in agreement and 1 think he understands that.
I would ask him to consider a couple of other points. Farmers are working over-all on a cash basis in the tax system. That is a tremendous asset for a farmer. In small or big business, an entrepreneur must use the accrual system, but a farmer has the benefit of the cash basis. That really helps a farmer over-all inside the system.
Of course, he can take advantage of an RRSP if he chooses to do so. He also has some intergenerational rollover provisions which are very helpful within a family, which again is unique to the farming community. In the April Budget we noticed some special new loss provisions for farmers, the ones who have just come through really tough times. We also added the 40 per cent refundable tax credit.
The Hon. Member should keep these other benefits in mind when zeroing in on the capital gains problem. Having said all that, I understand the difficulty that we are facing here. If a man works all of his life and is not particularly conversant with the tax system, he is not too aware of all of his liabilities. People who are workers, farmers and businessmen are not tax experts. For example, if a farmer works all his life, it hurts when he sells his farm and discovers that his retirement fund is diminished by 25 per cent. There is no denying that it hurts.
On the other hand, I would ask the Hon. Member to realize that others are also faced with that problem. We are in this difficult position where we have to try to consider how we can keep the tax system in a fair balance. While we do not want to distort it, neither do we want to create this kind of burden for a man out of a surprise. I suppose the only answer 1 can give is to counsel some degree of tax awareness and financial planning so that people are prepared for the capital gains tax when it happens.
It is an emotional issue. I understand the emotion behind it. 1 cannot agree with all of it because I think some of the alternatives, as I have tried to demonstrate here, would make things potentially worse for our economy. Therefore, I hope the Hon. Member will take that into consideration. We appreciate the input he has given us but 1 hope that he will look at some of the alternatives which might be much worse.

Mr. Chairman, I want to make one point which I think the Hon. Parliamentary Secretary misses entirely. It is wrong to charge capital gains tax on the value of land which it cannot repay. That is distortion of the worst kind, and that is the point I am trying to make. An average taken of all the land value does not represent the productive value at all. Surely the Government could accept the statement from a qualified evaluator saying that certain land will produce so much and should be valued at that amount. It should not be done by taking a figure out of a hat, as many of the officials in the Department of National Revenue are doing today, and not accepting the evaluated value. The officials should not simply say the value is $800 an acre or $500 an acre, as it is in the case I mentioned. The evaluator says that it will never repay any more than $200 per acre. That is what I want to emphasize, and when the Hon. Member considers this he will see that it is a distortion of the worst kind.
Question.

speechtext: The Hon. Member suggests we call it six o'clock.

December 19, 1983

according to his illustration, a very big concession to this group of people. He used the illustration of a person under the system with an income of $60. After the inflation factor was taken into account and the capital gains tax, which is half of the regular tax, the tax on the $60 income would be $3.50. This is a tax rate of under 6 per cent. I cannot think of a salary earner who would not like to have his tax at less than 6 per cent. Perhaps the Minister can explain tomorrow morning the justification for this.
