subtopic: SUPPLY AND SERVICES-PURCHASE OF AMERICAN COAL FOR USE AT CANADIAN FORCES BASE GAGETOWN, N.B. (B) REQUEST FOR AMENDMENT OF POLICY
SUPPLY AND SERVICES-PURCHASE OF AMERICAN COAL FOR USE AT CANADIAN FORCES BASE GAGETOWN, N.B. (B) REQUEST FOR AMENDMENT OF POLICY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my presentation today relates to a question 1 directed to the Minister of Supply and Services (Mr. Lapointe) on December 15, 1983 concerning the purchase of coal by his Department for the Department of National Defence for use at Canadian Forces Base Gagetown.
To put the question in context, let me explain the historical background. Canadian Forces Base Gagetown for many years utilized coal to produce its requirements for heat and other energy purposes. During that period of time the coal has normally been purchased from the Cape Breton Development Corporation which operates coal mines in Cape Breton, Nova Scotia and in some cases from the New Brunswick Coal Corporation which operates mines in Minto, New Brunswick, and in other places. I understand that over the years this coal supply contract was the subject of tenders and normally either the Cape Breton Development Corporation or the Minto mine would have the most acceptable tender.
1 understand that more recently in 1983 the coal contract was again put out to tender for the supply of approximately 17,500 tonnes of coal with no particular specifications and bids were accepted on that amount of coal. As it happened the successful bidder was not Cape Breton Coal Development Corporation or the Minto Corporation but another company which stipulated and eventually supplied coal mined in the State of Kentucky.
I became aware of this situation when I watched the news report that described the shipment of this amount of coal to the Port of Saint John. Not only do we have a Canadian
Adjournment Debate
Forces Base supplied with coal mined in the State of Kentucky, it was brought to this country on foreign marine carriers with all the expenses attendant upon that kind of transportation. Had the coal been purchased from Devco it would have been shipped from Cape Breton by Canadian National Railway or another local Canadian transporter. We are not only losing for the Canadian economy, and particularly the economy of Nova Scotia, the amount of the coal sale but we have lost the opportunity to transport that coal and all the other things connected with the supply of that amount of coal.
1 suppose the Minister of Supply and Services or the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Blais) who answered the question in the House on September 15, 1983 will respond that the Government made the best deal available at the time in response to the tender. Of course, that requires us to deal with the price of coal as supplied by the Cape Breton Development Corporation.
1 want to make the point very clearly, and I will be very interested in the Minister's reply, that there is more than price involved. Here we have the ludicrous situation of the Government of Canada, through the Department of Supply and Services, buying coal from a competitor of its own agency, the Cape Breton Development Corporation, adding in the result to the astounding deficit of that Crown agency.
Let me speak very briefly about the situation at the Cape Breton Development Corporation. Recently the President of the Corporation announced that the deficit of the Corporation for the current financial year would approximate $62 million. According to newspaper reports, this shocked the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Lumley), who is the Minister responsible for regional economic expansion, the Minister in charge of the Cape Breton Development Corporation.
Time and time again over the years the Auditor General has reported about transactions between the Cape Breton Development Corporation and the Government of Canada, complaining about the loose financial arrangements between the two emanations which in fact are principal and agent, the Cape Breton Development Corporation being a Crown agency. Any failings of the Cape Breton Development Corporation have to reflect back on the Government which is the sole owner of this organization. It has the sole and complete responsibility through its board of directors, which it appoints, for the operations of that organization.
It is no answer to say that the Government put the contract out for tender and awarded it to the lowest bidder in terms of price. That is not the issue. The issue is the relationship of the Government of Canada through its Crown agency, the Cape Breton Development Corporation, to all of those persons who are affected by their activities. The persons affected by this activity are the miners of Cape Breton who for years have worked diligently to preserve the operation of the Cape Breton coal mine as a viable enterprise.

December 19, 1983
Adjournment Debate
As a result of this decision on the part of the federal Government, those miners are deprived of the $1.3 million proceeds of the sale. That could have been used to decrease the deficit of the Cape Breton Development Corporation and pay the salaries to those miners. When you divide that $1.3 million by a wage in the area of $25,000 to $26,000 annually, that would employ 50 Cape Breton coal miners. 1 use that only to put the matter in perspective and to indicate how important this transaction is to people in Nova Scotia, particularly people in Cape Breton employed in the Cape Breton coal mines.

Mr. Speaker, I congratulate the Hon. Member for Halifax West (Mr. Crosby) who has suddenly found a great interest in and concern for the coal miners of Cape Breton. As a member on the Government side, I thank him for his interest and for verbalizing his real concerns in this matter as they relate to the development of the economy in Cape Breton.
Let me take the opportunity to inform the House and the general public that the Hon. Member is talking out of both sides of his mouth. He supports the Leader of the Conservative Party who says they want to reduce the deficit. However, when a Crown corporation comes to the forefront and he can make a bit of cheap political hay, he takes a different course. I say to the Hon. Member for Halifax West that there will be many opportunities of debate when he can outline his stand on a lot of issues.
The Hon. Member talked about a deficit of a Crown corporation administered by the Government of Canada. That Crown corporation is selling coal to a provincial Conservative Government in Nova Scotia and it is not receiving a fair price for the coal. If it were, the Hon. Member would not have the opportunity, the nerve or the audacity to stand in the House and condemn the Government of Canada. It is John Buchanan, the supporter of the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Mul-roney) and the Hon. Member for Halifax West, who will not under any circumstances give a fair and just price for Cape Breton coal.
Those are some of the facts, Mr. Speaker. The Hon. Member for Halifax West hides behind mirrors, just as does the Leader of the Opposition. In Calgary, the Leader of the Opposition gave one speech; in Nova Scotia, he gave another. The Hon. Member for Halifax West has the same attitude. In Cape Breton, he is all for the miners and wants to support them. When he is in the big Halifax Club in Halifax, what does he say? He says: "Damn the Cape Bretoners, we give them too much". That, Mr. Speaker, is where that Member stands when it comes to the price of coal.
I would like to add something else to the record, Mr. Speaker. This particular individual and his Party have advocated relationships with the United States time and time again. May I remind him of a GATT Agreement with the United States to which Canada is privy. Are we to break that agreement because the Leader of the Tory Party and what I
would call his "finker" from Halifax West say that we should now breach that particular agreement to suit a particular contract? The comments made by the Hon. Member are absolutely shameful. He is hypocritical. In addition, Mr. Speaker, he does not have the audacity to go to Cape Breton and share his so-called biased views with those people.

subtopic: TOURISM-TAX ON CANADIAN ADVERTISING LITERATURE-PROPOSED UNITED STATES LEGISLATION
TOURISM-TAX ON CANADIAN ADVERTISING LITERATURE-PROPOSED UNITED STATES LEGISLATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on December 15, I put a question to the Minister of State for Small Businesses and Tourism (Mr. Smith). I asked him whether he was conscious of the fact that there was a Bill before the United States House of Representatives which would impose a tax or a duty on Canadian tourist literature entering the United States. This Bill is sponsored by Congressman William J. Hughes from the Second District of New Jersey. If this Bill were to be passed, it would impose a tax on toursit literature entering the United States.
This Bill before the House of Representatives is very important to many areas of the country which depend upon tourists from the United States. Particularly in my own constituency which includes Sault-Ste-Marie, Algoma and Manitoulin, literally thousands of tourists come across the border each year for vacations in the various communities in the district.
A great deal of advertising done in the United States is by sportmen's groups, tourist associations and travel associations which attend the sportsmen's shows and the like in the American States of Ohio, Michigan and Missouri. Of course, the members of these associations take with them travel brochures and so on. In fact, last year, the Government of Canada, through the employment-related initiatives program, sponsored a program of tourist promotion for our area throughout the northern mid-western states to the tune of $119,000. The people involved with this program took with them some 60,000 brochures related to this one single promotion for the Manitoulin Tourist Association.
If this Bill before the United States Congress were to pass, it seems that a duty would be imposed on these brochures. The people from these associations go to the mid-western states for these annual travel and tourist shows. If United States House of Representatives Bill No. 4074 were to impose a 9 per cent or 10 per cent travel sales tax or duty similar to the kind of sales tax we have on American literature entering Canada, this would, of course, represent a serious expenditure for these associations from Canada which go to the United States to promote their industry. This industry has been suffering in the last year or two with the downturn in the North American economy.
I put my question to the Minister of State for Small Businesses and Tourism, and suggested that when the Minister of Finance (Mr. Lalonde) brings in his next budget, which I anticipate within two or three months, he consider dropping the 9 per cent sales tax on tourist promotional literature which
December 19, 1983

comes across the border from the United States. If that were done 1 am sure the proposed Bill, which is apparently designed to retaliate against our present tax, would likewise be dropped. The International Association of Travel Exhibitors has written to many tourist operators in my constituency pointing out that the Bill is likely to be passed in the House of Representatives unless some action is taken on the 9 per cent sales tax proposed by Canada on its travel information.
I suggest to the Parliamentary Secretary that with all his power and the perogatives of his position he should be able to say to the Minister of Finance-and perhaps he could make a commitment to do so this afternoon-that in the next budget he should drop this sales tax and thus avoid retaliatory action by the House of Representatives in Washington.

speakeroldname: Mr. Douglas Fisher (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
subtopic: TOURISM-TAX ON CANADIAN ADVERTISING LITERATURE-PROPOSED UNITED STATES LEGISLATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my good friend, the Hon. Member for Algoma (Mr. Foster), has once again represented the interests of his constituency in an outstanding fashion. I am sure the people there in the tourist industry are proud of the representations he has made in the House on their behalf. 1 can assure them that he does this consistently in his role as chairman of the Ontario caucus and in his activities as a private Member in the chamber.
Our concern is that the issue has been somewhat misunderstood by the Americans and is being blown out of all proportion. We are quite anxious to see that it is well understood by people on all sides. The 9 per cent federal sales tax is generally applied to most goods that are either manufactured in Canada or imported. It is quite important to understand that fact. Until two years ago, Revenue Canada informally allowed some importation of tourist brochures, partly on the basis that it was such a small activity and partly because much of the material had no commercial value. It then become clear that there is a degree of unintended discrimination taking place. A Canadian businessman could have his material prepared and printed in the United States. It could then be imported to Canada, thereby escaping the 9 per cent tax which everyone else has to pay.
It is important to note that problem of discrimination. We were merely trying to even out the application of the tax so that it was fair to everyone. The tourist operator who imported material would be given the same privileges and would pay the same taxes as the tourist operator who had the material printed in Canada. We have been quite careful to inform the Americans of this. I am told that the American ambassador, His Excellency Paul Robinson, has been in touch with the Minister of Finance about the matter. The Minister apparently has taken the opportunity to explain that this is not intended as an attack on American material but is intended to even out our own domestic taxation.
There has been some question about non-profit materials and about the type of activity that is taxed. Sometimes government materials are being taxed. We have pointed out to the Americans that non-profit groups in Canada pay the tax. This is not a case where we are singling out a worthy group for some form of punishment.
Adjournment Debate
So, within that context, I would make it clear to the Hon. Member that the tax is not intended as a punishment to his constituent. It is certainly not intended as a deterrent to the American printer, American exhibitor or the American tourist operator. We are simply trying to ensure fair application of the tax inside Canada. I will certainly take the representations the Hon. Member has made about the Budget. However, I am not the Minister of Finance so my commitments would not be too meaningful in that regard.

LABOUR RELATIONS-INTRODUCTION OF NEW TECHNOLOGY-REQUEST FOR WORKERS' BARGAINING RIGHTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, one year ago the Catholic Bishops said that unemployment was the most urgent problem facing Canada. Canadians agreed. More than 1.5 million Canadians remain unemployed, many of them young people and women. Unemployment continues to hurt men and women in this country who suffer increasingly from mental illness, family breakdown, the high cost of living, while they lose confidence and skills. Needless to say, any man or woman who is unemployed and looking for a job received nothing from the Throne Speech on December 7. The overwhelming failure of this Liberal Government is in its lack of commitment to jobs, its lack of a comprehensive strategy to get Canadians back to work and its refusal to accept full employment as a national goal.
On December 9 I had hoped to question the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) on his lack of commitment to full employment for Canadians. However, neither he nor most of the senior Cabinet Ministers were in the House at the time to be accountable to the people of Canada. I therefore asked the Minister of State for Economic Development (Mr. Johnston) to establish full employment as a national priority goal for Canada. He alleged that every program, every project, has been directed to that very need and that 350,000 new jobs have been created in the past year. He conveniently neglected to mention that unemployment continues at more than 11 per cent in Canada and that 1.3 million fulltime jobs have disappeared since August, 1981.
I urged the Government and the Minister to follow the example of European countries such as Sweden and Austria which have successfully established full employment as a national goal and as a result have reduced unemployment below 3 per cent. The Minister of State for Economic Development tried to deflect the issue by referring to the Soviet Union. I would suggest, Mr. Speaker, that it is far more relevant to make comparisons to social democratic countries with similar parliamentary traditions to our own, as I did. The Minister, with typical Liberal blindness, also ignored in his answer the social costs of unemployment which have been documented recently by the Canadian Mental Health Association. Their report is a stark indictment of the Government's lack of action to create jobs and the impact it is having on people and their families.

December 19, 1983
Adjournment Debate
The Minister of Employment and Immigration (Mr. Roberts) said that the Throne Speech promises it will assist
125,000	adults and youth. This means only one job for every ten people, however, who are looking for work. For the 780,000 jobless adults the measures announced in the Throne Speech, plus those already in existence, will provide help to only 35,000, or one out of every 22 unemployed adults. Many of these adults are trying to feed families. The $1 billion program for youth is, in fact, little more than the amount which was allocated for youth earlier this year.
I also tried to question the Minister on the impact of technological change which is adding to unemployment. This Government intends to aid in the development of high tech industries, and we do not object to this, but it provides no protection or alternative areas of work for workers who are going to be displaced by new technology. Women in traditional office jobs are the first victims to go. We in the NDP believe that workers must be involved in the planning and timing of technological change which will affect them. They must have options for retraining or other alternate kinds of work.
I have urged the Government to assist in expanding a range of community service jobs and co-operatives as one alternate type of job sector. 1 have also asked for benefits and protections for part-time workers, more flexible and earlier pensions, and increased family benefits to ease the stress of unemployment.
The NDP will never accept 10 per cent or 11 per cent unemployment as a given in a country which has an unlimited potential to employ its human resources more productively. Other countries are planning for human needs in a time of massive change and so must we. Canada must invest in people and permanent jobs rather than paying the high cost of unemployment insurance, welfare and social disintegration.
Technology must serve the needs of the people, rather than making them subservient to technology. We are particularly concerned by the projections that women will bear the brunt of the negative employment effects of new technology and of course this is already happening.
In Women and the Chip, Heather Menzies predicts that the unemployment rate among female clerical workers could escalate as high as 33 per cent by 1990. These women are among the most vulnerable of all workers.
The NDP has specific proposals to deal with technological change, including amendments to the Canada Labour Code to provide a model for provincial legislation with respect to technological change, and to provide a framework for the introduction of technology where workers are unorganized. This should include involvement of workers in decisions on the introduction of new technology, making the introduction of technological change a negotiable item in contracts, and providing a minimum of six months to one year notice when technological change is contemplated. Where workers are unorganized, joint technology committees should be set up in
any workplace with 50 or more employees to consult and bargain over the introduction of new technology.
We also propose that progress be made towards shortening the hours of work by shortening the work week, paid educational leave, providing longer annual holidays and optional early retirement.
We would vastly expand opportunities for retraining of workers affected by technological change, with assistance from both Government and employers. The levy grant system is one method to ensure that employers pay their share of the country's training needs.
Finally, it is essential that the Government plan with provinces and with people for alternate areas of work. We have unlimited needs and potential jobs in the arts, literature, research, community services, food production and environmental projects, to name only a few. If the Government implemented these recommendations it would go a long way toward counteracting unemployment.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, regarding the concerns expressed by the Hon. Member, I would like to take this opportunity to point out that the Canada Labour Code is in the forefront of Canadian labour legislation on the matter of establishing the right to negotiate technological change. If the collective agreement contains no specific provisions to help employees affected by technological change and no alternative method to resolve disputes arising from technological change exists, the Canada Labour Code provides for sending a notice to negotiate and for negotiations as soon as an employer makes known his intention to introduce significant technological change. With the approval of the Canada Labour Relations Board, it is then even possible to reopen negotiations on a current collective agreement, and the employer cannot introduce any changes until agreement has been reached or the conciliation process has been completed.
When these provisions were adopted by Parliament in 1972, they were considered to be radical by many corporate leaders and businessmen. Up to now, only three provinces have adopted provisions on technological change. The purpose of the provincial legislation is the same as in the case of the federal legislation: to give both parties specific responsibility for negotiating conditions of implementation that will keep the impact of technological change on the employees affected to a minimum.
Mr. Speaker, our experience in applying the federal provisions has shown that the parties act responsibly and approach the issue of technological change through the collective bargaining process. We are convinced that the method adopted by
December 19, 1983

Parliament in 1972 is the right one and that we have achieved our objective which consisted in facilitating the introduction of technological advances while protecting employees against any infringement on their rights.
